title: How plants send and receive signals, and whether plants feel, learn and remember

summary.text: A caterpillar chews a maize leaf deep inside the plant, where nobody can see. Over the next hours tiny wasps arrive, find the hidden caterpillar and lay their eggs in them. How did the wasps know? The chewed plant gave off a smell, and the wasps followed that smell. Plants send signals through their own bodies, through the air, and from their roots into the soil. Most plants also live joined to fungi, and scientists are testing whether food and warnings pass between plants along the fungal threads. Your child tests whether a torn leaf can be found by smell alone, and whether a daily stroke changes how seedlings grow. Then they weigh the evidence in an argument that scientists are still having: do plants feel, learn and remember?
summary.art: A young maize plant with a ragged hole in one leaf, a faint trail of smell drifting from the hole on the wind, and two tiny black wasps flying along the trail towards the plant.

intro.hook: A caterpillar bites one leaf of a plant. Two minutes later, leaves on the far side of the plant begin to switch on their defences. No caterpillar has touched those leaves. A plant has no nerves. So how did the far leaves get the news?
intro.text: Scientists filmed the answer in 2018, and you will read it in this unit. The news travelled inside the plant as a wave of electric charge and chemicals. A plant also sends news out of their body. Some goes into the air as smells, and some goes into the soil from the roots. Other living beings receive that news: neighbouring plants, insects, fungi and you. You start with your own nose. In the first activity, the Torn Leaf Test, you find out whether a leaf gives off something new when it is damaged.
intro.art: A small plant drawn in outline with one leaf bitten by a caterpillar, and a glowing wave travelling along the leaf veins towards a leaf on the other side.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a signal is, and name the sender, the carrier and the receiver in a plant example.
By the end I can describe three paths for plant signals: inside the plant, through the air, and from the roots into the soil.
By the end I can explain what a mycorrhiza is, and what the plant and the fungus each give.
By the end I can run a fair touch test with a control cup, ten seedlings in each cup, a mean and a chart.
By the end I can explain how a short touch can change a plant's growth for days.
By the end I can give evidence that plants keep information about their past, and say why scientists argue about the words learn, remember and feel.
By the end I can say what an experiment must rule out before we accept its claim, and why other scientists must repeat it.
By the end I can say what is still unknown about fungal networks and about what plants feel.

terms.meaning: A stimulus is anything a living being can sense: a touch, light, a chemical, warmth or damage. For more than one we say stimuli.
terms.example: A caterpillar's bite is a stimulus for a maize plant.
terms.art: A caterpillar biting the edge of a leaf, with a small star at the bite.

terms.meaning: A response is what a living being does because of a stimulus.
terms.example: A touch-me-not folding their leaflets after a touch is a response.
terms.art: A touch-me-not leaf half folded, with a finger moving away.

terms.meaning: A signal is something that carries news from one place to another and changes what the receiver does. Every signal has a sender, a carrier and a receiver.
terms.example: The smell of a chewed maize leaf is a signal. The leaf is the sender, the air is the carrier and a wasp is one receiver.
terms.art: A leaf, a wavy line of smell and a wasp, labelled sender, carrier and receiver.

terms.meaning: A receptor is a tiny part of a cell that fits one kind of stimulus, as a lock fits one key. When the right thing arrives, the receptor starts a change inside the cell.
terms.example: Your nose has receptors for smell chemicals. A plant's cells have receptors for light, touch and many chemicals.
terms.art: A cell surface with a small cup-shaped receptor and a matching shape settling into it.

terms.meaning: A hormone is a chemical that one part of a living body makes and another part responds to. It is a signal that stays inside the body.
terms.example: Jasmonic acid is a plant hormone. Damaged leaves make it, and it switches on the making of defence chemicals.
terms.art: A plant with a small dot travelling up the stem from a damaged leaf to a healthy leaf.

terms.meaning: An electrical signal is a wave of electric charge that passes from cell to cell. Charged particles called ions move in and out of each cell in turn.
terms.example: A touch-me-not leaf folds because an electrical signal runs along it at 2 to 3 centimetres a second.
terms.art: A row of plant cells with a small lightning mark moving from one cell to the next.

terms.meaning: A volatile is a chemical that turns into a gas easily and drifts through the air. Every smell is made of volatiles.
terms.example: The smell of freshly cut grass is a mix of volatiles that grass leaves make when they are cut.
terms.art: A cut blade of grass with small dots drifting up from the cut end.

terms.meaning: A root exudate is any chemical that a living root lets out into the soil. Roots let out sugars, acids and signal chemicals.
terms.example: Root exudates from a jowar plant tell nearby fungi that a root is close.
terms.art: A root tip in soil with small dots spreading out from it into the soil water.

terms.meaning: A hypha is one thread of a fungus. It is a tube far thinner than a hair. For more than one we say hyphae (say 'high-fee').
terms.example: The white fluff on old bread is a tangle of hyphae.
terms.art: A magnified view of branching white threads growing across a crumb of bread.

terms.meaning: A mycelium is the whole body of a fungus, made of all their hyphae together. It lives hidden in soil, wood or food.
terms.example: A mushroom is only the fruit of a fungus. The mycelium below the ground is the main body.
terms.art: A mushroom above ground with a wide web of fine white threads spreading below it in the soil.

terms.meaning: A mycorrhiza is a partnership between the roots of a plant and a fungus. The word means 'fungus-root'. Say 'my-ko-rye-za'.
terms.example: A mango tree's roots are joined to fungi. The fungi bring water and minerals, and the tree gives them sugar.
terms.art: A tree root with fine fungal threads growing from it out into the soil, with arrows showing sugar going one way and minerals the other.

terms.meaning: A common mycorrhizal network is a web of fungal threads that is joined to the roots of two or more plants at once.
terms.example: In a pot, two tomato plants can be joined underground by the threads of one fungus.
terms.art: Two plants side by side with their roots linked underground by one web of fine threads.

terms.meaning: Thigmomorphogenesis is the change in a plant's shape caused by touch or shaking. Touched plants grow shorter and thicker. Say 'thig-mo-mor-fo-jen-e-sis'.
terms.example: A tree on a windy hilltop is shorter and thicker than the same kind of tree in a sheltered valley.
terms.art: Two trees of one kind: a tall thin one in a calm valley and a short thick one bent by wind on a hilltop.

terms.meaning: Habituation means responding less and less to a stimulus that keeps coming and does no harm. It is the simplest kind of learning.
terms.example: You stop noticing the sound of the ceiling fan after a few minutes.
terms.art: A child reading calmly under a whirring ceiling fan.

terms.meaning: Priming means that a plant who has met a danger once responds faster and more strongly the next time.
terms.example: A maize seedling that has smelled a damaged neighbour makes defence chemicals faster when a caterpillar arrives.
terms.art: Two maize seedlings with a caterpillar on each, one with a small shield mark that is larger than the other's.

terms.meaning: A control is the part of an experiment where you do not make the change you are testing. Everything else is kept the same, so you have something to compare with.
terms.example: In the Touch Test, the cup of seedlings that nobody strokes is the control.
terms.art: Two cups of seedlings on a windowsill, one with a hand above it and one labelled 'control'.

terms.meaning: To replicate an experiment is to do it again, often in another laboratory, to see whether the same result comes out.
terms.example: In 2020 a scientist tried to replicate a test of learning in pea plants, and did not get the same result.
terms.art: Two scientists in different rooms, each with the same row of pea plants and a notebook.

explanations.definition: A signal is something that carries news from a sender to a receiver and changes what the receiver does. The thing that carries it is called the carrier.
explanations.description: A plant senses many kinds of stimulus: light, gravity, touch, water, warmth, chemicals and damage. To sense a stimulus, a cell needs a receptor that fits it. But sensing in one place is not enough. A root that finds dry soil is far from the leaves that lose the water. So the news must travel, and whatever carries it is a signal. To understand any signal, ask three questions. Who sent it? What carried it? Who received it, and what did they do then? The third question matters most. A smell that changes nobody's behaviour is not acting as a signal. The same smell becomes a signal when someone has a receptor for it and responds.
examples: A caterpillar bites a leaf. The bitten leaf is the sender, a wave of electric charge is the carrier, and far leaves are the receivers. They respond by getting their defences ready.
A ripe banana gives off the gas ethylene. The air carries it, and a raw mango nearby responds by ripening sooner.
In the Torn Leaf Test, the torn leaf is the sender, the air is the carrier and your nose is the receiver.
explanations.art: A simple diagram of a bitten leaf labelled 'sender', an arrow labelled 'carrier' and a far leaf labelled 'receiver'.

explanations.definition: Inside a plant, news travels as electrical signals that pass from cell to cell, and as hormones that move in the plant's sap.
explanations.description: Every living cell keeps more of some charged particles inside than outside. Charged particles are called ions. Because of this, there is a small electric voltage across the skin of every cell. In a plant cell the voltage is between one and two tenths of a volt. When a caterpillar bites a leaf, the broken cells spill a chemical called glutamate. The next cells have receptors for glutamate. Those cells open tiny gates, and calcium ions rush in. That change makes the cells after them do the same, so a wave travels along the veins. In 2018 Masatsugu Toyota and Simon Gilroy filmed this wave in thale cress, a small relative of mustard. They used plants that glow wherever calcium rises. The wave moved at about 1 millimetre a second and reached far leaves within one or two minutes. There the leaves began to make the hormone jasmonic acid, which switches on the making of defence chemicals. This is much slower than your nerves, which carry signals at up to 100 metres a second. But a caterpillar takes many minutes to eat one leaf, so the news arrives in time.
examples: A touch-me-not folds because an electrical signal runs along the leaf at 2 to 3 centimetres a second. J.C. Bose measured such signals in Kolkata more than a hundred years ago.
A Venus flytrap's trap snaps shut when an electrical signal crosses it. You can read about this under 'Plants keep information about their past'.
When roots meet dry soil, they send a hormone up to the leaves. The leaves respond by closing their tiny air holes, which saves water.
explanations.art: A small plant seen from above, with a bright wave spreading from a bitten leaf along the veins to the other leaves, and a clock showing two minutes.

explanations.definition: A damaged plant gives off volatiles, which are chemicals that drift through the air as smells. Other living beings that have receptors for those volatiles respond to them.
explanations.description: Some leaf smells are stored in advance. Curry leaves, tulsi and mint keep scented oils in tiny pockets, and tearing the leaf bursts the pockets. Other smells are made fresh. Within seconds of being cut, the cells of a grass blade or a palak leaf start making 'green leaf volatiles', the smell of cut grass. A cabbage or radish leaf makes sharp mustard oils only when their cells are broken. Hours after a caterpillar starts feeding, a plant makes a further mix of volatiles. In 1990 Ted Turlings and his team showed that maize plants do this when caterpillar spit touches the wound. A plain cut gives a much weaker smell. Tiny wasps follow that smell and lay their eggs inside the caterpillars. The young wasps then eat the caterpillars. Other plants receive these volatiles too. In 2000 Richard Karban found that wild tobacco plants growing near clipped sagebrush bushes were eaten less by insects. Later tests showed why. Plants that receive damage volatiles get their own defences ready, which is called priming.
examples: The smell of a freshly mown cricket ground is the grass leaves' damage volatiles.
Dodder is a yellow thread-like plant that lives on other plants. In 2006 Consuelo De Moraes and her team showed that dodder seedlings grow towards the smell of a tomato plant.
A lima bean plant uses their own damage volatiles as an inside signal too. The smell travels through the air from a damaged leaf to other leaves of the same plant.
explanations.art: A chewed maize plant with a trail of smell dots drifting to a neighbouring maize plant and to a small wasp in the air.

explanations.concept: Mycorrhiza: plants and fungi live joined together
explanations.definition: A mycorrhiza is a partnership between a plant's roots and a fungus. The fungus brings water and minerals to the plant, and the plant gives sugars and fats to the fungus.
explanations.description: The body of a fungus is a mass of fine threads called hyphae. Each thread is many times thinner than a hair, so it can enter gaps in the soil that are too narrow for any root. In a mycorrhiza the threads grow into or around the plant's roots and far out into the soil. Why do the two live together? A fungus has no chlorophyll, so they cannot make food from light. A plant can. But a plant's roots reach only a small part of the soil. Phosphorus is a mineral every cell needs, and it hardly moves in soil. The fungal threads reach it and carry it back. In return the plant gives the fungus food, often about a tenth of all the food the plant makes. More than eight of every ten kinds of land plant live this way, including mango, coconut, banana, ragi, pine and sal. A few, such as mustard, cabbage and palak, do without fungi. Fossils about 400 million years old show fungal threads inside some of the first land plants. Many scientists think that fungi helped plants to live on land before plants had proper roots.
examples: Rugra is a round mushroom sold in the markets of Ranchi in the monsoon. It is the fruit of a fungus that lives joined to the roots of sal trees. People gather it from sal forests.
An orchid seed is as fine as dust and carries almost no food. In the wild, an orchid seed can grow only after a fungus enters and feeds them.

In 1885 the German scientist Albert Bernhard Frank gave mycorrhiza its name. Many scientists then thought fungi on roots were a disease. Frank said the fungi were feeding the trees, and later experiments showed he was right.
explanations.art: A cut-away view of soil showing a tree root wrapped in fine white threads that spread far out between the soil grains, with a small arrow labelled 'sugar' pointing to the fungus and one labelled 'water and minerals' pointing to the root.

explanations.concept: Signals from roots into the soil
explanations.definition: Roots let out chemicals called root exudates into the soil. Fungi, bacteria and other plants that have receptors for those chemicals respond to them.
explanations.description: A plant spends real food on root exudates, so these chemicals must matter to the plant. Some of them call partners. A root that is short of phosphorus lets out chemicals called strigolactones. The threads of mycorrhizal fungi sense them and branch towards the root. Kohki Akiyama and his team showed this in 2005. The roots of beans and other dals let out different chemicals that call the bacteria who live in their root swellings. But any signal put into the soil can be received by others too. Witchweed is a small plant that lives by tapping the roots of jowar, bajra and sugarcane. A witchweed seed can lie in the soil for years. They sprout only when they sense strigolactones, because that means a root is close enough to reach. So the plant's call to a helpful fungus is also the wake-up call for a plant that will steal from them. Roots also pass on news of trouble. In 2011 Omer Falik and his team in Israel kept one pea plant short of water. Neighbours who shared soil with that plant's roots closed their leaf holes within an hour, though they had plenty of water themselves.
examples: Farmers sometimes sow cotton in a field full of witchweed seeds. Cotton roots make the seeds sprout, but witchweed cannot live on cotton, so the seedlings die.
A sandalwood tree's roots join on to the roots of neighbouring plants and take water and minerals from them. So growers plant a sandalwood seedling beside a host plant such as tur.

A sea rocket is a small beach plant. In one study from 2007, sea rockets grew more roots beside strangers than beside sisters and brothers. Other scientists are still testing whether plants can tell family from strangers.
explanations.art: A cut-away view of soil with a jowar root giving off dots, a fungal thread branching towards the root, and a tiny witchweed seed nearby beginning to sprout.

explanations.concept: Do food and warnings pass between plants through fungal threads?
explanations.definition: A common mycorrhizal network is a web of fungal threads joined to two or more plants. Scientists agree that such networks exist. They disagree about how much food and news passes through them from plant to plant in a real forest.
explanations.description: Some facts are settled. Ghost plants are white, with no chlorophyll at all, so they cannot make food. They get all their sugar from fungi that are joined to nearby trees. So sugar that a tree made can reach another plant through a fungus. In 1997 Suzanne Simard fed marked carbon dioxide to birch trees in a Canadian forest. Some of the marked carbon turned up in fir trees nearby, and shaded firs received more. The science journal Nature called this the 'wood-wide web'. In pots, a warning seems to pass as well. In 2010 Yuan Yuan Song and her team joined tomato plants by fungal threads and infected one plant with a leaf disease. The healthy partners switched on their defence genes. In 2013 Zdenka Babikova and her team did a similar test with bean plants and aphids. When a fine mesh stopped the threads from joining the plants, no warning arrived. The argument is about real forests. Does enough food move to matter to a seedling? Does the news go through the threads, or through the soil water beside them? Does a tree 'send' anything, or does the fungus move food to suit themself? Nobody has shown the answers yet.
examples: A ghost plant under Himalayan forest trees is white from top to bottom. All their food comes through fungal threads from the trees around them.
In the game Under the Forest, you play the idea that big trees feed shaded seedlings through the threads. Then you play the critics' idea and compare.
To test the path, scientists bury plants in bags of mesh. One mesh lets fungal threads through but stops roots. A finer mesh stops the threads but lets water through.

perspectives.who: Suzanne Simard, a forest scientist in Canada
perspectives.explanation: Old trees are joined by fungi to many younger ones. Food and warnings move through the threads, and seedlings in deep shade do better when they are joined to the network. Foresters should leave the big old trees standing.

perspectives.who: Justine Karst, Melanie Jones and Jason Hoeksema, who reviewed the forest studies in 2023
perspectives.explanation: The networks are real, but the popular story has run ahead of the evidence. Very few forest studies have mapped a network. The amounts of food found moving were small. In many tests, seedlings joined to a network grew no better, and some grew worse.

perspectives.who: Toby Kiers and other scientists who study the fungi
perspectives.explanation: Ask what the fungus gains. A fungus is a living being with their own needs, not a pipe. In laboratory tests, fungi send more minerals to the roots that pay them more sugar. Food may move because it suits the fungus.

explanations.art: Two forest trees joined underground by a web of threads, with a question mark over a small arrow drawn along the threads from the big tree to a seedling.

explanations.concept: How a touch changes the way a plant grows
explanations.definition: A plant that is touched, bent or shaken again and again grows shorter and thicker. This change is called thigmomorphogenesis.
explanations.description: In the Touch Test, each stroke lasts about a second, yet the seedlings change over a week. Here is what happens in between. Plant cells have touch receptors in their skins. When a stem bends, these receptors open and calcium ions flow into the cells. Within about half an hour, that switches on a group of genes called touch genes. A gene is an instruction for building one of the cell's working parts. Janet Braam found the touch genes in 1990, by accident. She sprayed plants with a hormone, and found that the plants sprayed with plain water changed as well. The spray itself was a touch. The touched plant then makes less gibberellin, the hormone that makes stems grow long. The plant also builds thicker cell walls. Why would this help a plant? A stem that keeps being bent is probably growing in a windy place. A short, thick stem is much harder to snap than a tall, thin one. So the plant changes their growth to suit the place they are in. The scientist Mark Jaffe gave the change its long name in 1973.
examples: Trees on a windy sea coast or hilltop grow shorter and thicker than the same kind of tree in a sheltered place.
In Japan, farmers have long walked over young wheat and barley plants in winter. The trodden plants grow sturdier. The custom is called mugifumi.
A young tree tied tightly to a stake cannot sway. The trunk stays thin, and the tree may fall when the stake is taken away.
explanations.art: Two cups of moong seedlings side by side, one tall and thin, the other shorter with thicker stems and a hand sweeping gently across the tops.

explanations.concept: Plants keep information about their past
explanations.definition: A plant's response today can depend on what happened to the plant minutes, weeks or months ago. So the plant's body holds information about the past.
explanations.description: Here are three cases that scientists agree on. The first lasts seconds. A Venus flytrap is a plant that catches insects in a trap made of two leaf halves. One touch on a trap hair does not shut the trap. A second touch within about 30 seconds does. The first touch raises the calcium inside the trap cells, and the calcium fades slowly. A second touch that comes in time adds enough to pass the level that shuts the trap. So the trap counts to two, and avoids closing on a raindrop. The second case lasts months. Cabbage and carrot plants flower only after they have been through weeks of cold. The cold slowly sticks chemical tags on to one gene, the gene that blocks flowering, and the tags switch that gene off. The tags stay in place when warm days return, so the plant flowers in spring. That is why seed for these vegetables is grown in the cool hills. The third case is priming. A plant that has been attacked once responds faster the next time. In each case something in the plant's body changed and stayed changed. Whether to call this 'remembering' is argued over, and the next card gives the views.
examples: A flytrap closes when a fly touches the trap hairs twice within about half a minute. Five or more touches start the digestive juices flowing.
Most kinds of cabbage grown all year in a hot place make leaves but no flowers, because the plants have had no winter.
A bean plant in a dark cupboard still lifts and lowers their leaves at about the right times for a few days. Earlier days set the plant's inside clock.
explanations.art: A Venus flytrap with a fly touching one trap hair and a small counter beside it showing '1', then '2' as the trap closes.

explanations.definition: To learn is to change what you do because of what has happened to you, in a way that lasts. Scientists are still arguing about whether experiments have shown this in plants.
explanations.description: Plants learn. In 2014 Monica Gagliano dropped potted touch-me-nots 15 centimetres on to foam, again and again. At first the plants folded their leaves. After many drops, they stopped folding. Were the plants just worn out? She tested that by shaking the same plants sideways, and they folded at once. So they still had the energy to fold. They had stopped only for the harmless drop. Many plants still did not fold for a drop 28 days later. This fits the definition of habituation, the simplest kind of learning. In 2016 Gagliano reported a harder kind of learning. Pea seedlings were given a breeze from a fan and then light from the same side, many times. Afterwards, she reported, the seedlings grew towards the fan even with no light. In 2020 Kasey Markel repeated that test with more plants and did not get the same result. So the first kind of learning has good evidence, and the second kind is in doubt until someone replicates it.
examples: You stop noticing a ticking clock. That is habituation, and it shows that even the simplest learning is useful: it saves effort.
In the Drop Test in this unit, you can repeat Monica Gagliano's first experiment if you have a touch-me-not.
In the activity Learned or Tired?, you work out which results fit each explanation.

perspectives.who: Monica Gagliano, who did the experiments
perspectives.explanation: The plants changed what they did because of experience, and the change lasted for weeks. In any animal we would call that learning and memory, so we should use the same words for a plant.

perspectives.who: Critics such as Lincoln Taiz and his co-authors
perspectives.explanation: The touch-me-not result may be a change in the leaf's folding parts, with nothing like a memory behind it. The word 'learning' should be kept for animals with nerve cells until much stronger evidence comes.

perspectives.who: Kasey Markel, who repeated the pea experiment
perspectives.explanation: The question is a fair one for science, and the way to answer it is to repeat the tests carefully. The pea result did not come out again, so for now it should not be counted as shown.

explanations.art: A potted touch-me-not falling a short way on to a cushion, with the leaves staying open, and beside it the same pot being shaken sideways with the leaves folded.

explanations.definition: To feel is to have an experience, such as pain or comfort, and not only to respond. Nobody has found a way to measure feeling directly in any being.
explanations.description: Plants feel, remember and decide. Here is what can be measured. A plant has receptors for touch, light, gravity, warmth, many chemicals and damage. The plant sends electrical signals, as your nerves do, and uses some of the same signal chemicals, such as glutamate. The gases that put people to sleep for an operation also work on plants. A touch-me-not kept in ether fumes stops folding, and so does a Venus flytrap. When the fumes clear, the plant responds again. What nobody can measure is the feeling itself. This is true for people as well. You cannot measure what a friend feels. You judge it from what she does and says, and from the fact that her body is like yours. A plant's body is very unlike yours, so that second clue is missing, and scientists read the evidence in different ways.
examples: J.C. Bose showed in the early 1900s that a touch-me-not given chloroform stops responding, and recovers in fresh air, as an animal does.
A plant responds differently to a caterpillar's bite and to a clean cut, so plants tell kinds of damage apart.
Roots growing through soil turn away from salt and towards water, and they weigh the two against each other.

perspectives.who: J.C. Bose, and today Paco Calvo, Monica Gagliano and Stefano Mancuso
perspectives.explanation: Plants sense, signal, choose and learn with their whole bodies. Feeling does not need a brain, just as breathing does not need lungs. A plant takes in air through tiny holes instead.

perspectives.who: Lincoln Taiz and seven other scientists, writing in 2019
perspectives.explanation: In animals, feeling goes with brains of a certain size and kind. Plants have nothing like that, and their responses can be explained without feeling. To them, calling a plant conscious adds a guess and explains nothing new.
Nobody yet knows how any body gives rise to feeling, not even a human brain. Until we know that, we have no test that can settle the question for plants, and both sides should say so.

explanations.art: A touch-me-not under a glass jar with a small cloud of fumes, leaves open and still while a pencil touches them through a gap, and beside it the same plant in fresh air with folded leaves.

explanations.concept: Why plants and animals signal in similar ways
explanations.definition: Plants and animals both signal with moving ions and with chemicals such as glutamate. The best explanation is that both inherited these tools from a shared ancestor.
explanations.description: Follow a signal down to the smallest scale and it is made of atoms carrying electric charge. A calcium ion is a calcium atom that has lost two electrons. A cell uses energy from food to pump ions out, as you might pump water up to a tank. When a gate opens, the ions rush back in, and that rush is the signal. Bacteria, fungi, plants and animals all do this. Plants and animals last shared an ancestor more than a billion years ago. That ancestor was a single cell. Plants have glutamate receptors built on the same plan as the ones in your brain. So scientists think this kind of signalling is older than both plants and animals. Nerves and brains came later, as one way of doing it fast. This last step is an idea drawn from comparing living things today. Nobody can test the signals of a being who lived a billion years ago.
examples: Glutamate carries signals between the nerve cells in your brain. In a plant, glutamate from broken cells starts the warning wave.
Fungal threads carry electrical pulses too. Scientists do not yet know what the pulses do.
Even a bacterium senses chemicals with receptors and swims towards food.
explanations.art: A simple family tree with one single cell at the bottom, branching up to a plant, a mushroom and a child, with the same small gate-and-ion symbol drawn beside each.

agreed.text: News of damage travels through a plant's body within minutes, as electrical and chemical signals.
agreed.evidence: In 2018 Toyota and Gilroy filmed waves of calcium crossing glowing plants after a caterpillar's bite. J.C. Bose recorded electrical signals in plants from 1901 onwards.

agreed.text: Damaged plants give off volatiles, and insects and other plants respond to them.
agreed.evidence: Turlings and his team showed in 1990 that wasps follow the smell of caterpillar-chewed maize. Field and laboratory tests since 2000 show that neighbouring plants prime their defences.

agreed.text: Most land plants live joined to fungi, and both partners gain.
agreed.evidence: The fungal threads can be seen in roots under a microscope. When phosphorus or carbon is marked, it can be followed from fungus to plant and from plant to fungus.

agreed.text: Sugar made by one plant can reach another plant through fungal threads.
agreed.evidence: Ghost plants have no chlorophyll and live only on sugar from fungi joined to trees. Marked carbon fed to one tree has been found in a neighbour.

agreed.text: Repeated touch makes plants grow shorter and thicker.
agreed.evidence: This has been measured in dozens of kinds of plant since Mark Jaffe's tests in 1973. Plant nurseries brush seedlings to keep them sturdy.

agreed.text: A plant's response can depend on events long past, such as a winter.
agreed.evidence: Plants that need cold before flowering stay leafy for years without it. The chemical tags that the cold leaves on one gene have been found and measured.

challenging.claim: Plants grow better when people play them music or speak kindly to them.
challenging.who: A popular belief, spread by the 1973 book The Secret Life of Plants
challenging.for: Plants do sense vibrations. In 2014 Heidi Appel and Rex Cocroft played thale cress plants a recording of a caterpillar chewing. Those plants later made more defence chemicals than plants kept in silence.
challenging.against: The music tests from the 1970s were not fair tests. The plants differed in light and warmth, and nobody measured without knowing which plant was which. Careful repeats found no effect of music or kind words.
challenging.context: This card is about a popular belief: that music or kind words help plants grow.

challenging.claim: Big old trees feed their own seedlings through fungal threads.
challenging.who: Suzanne Simard and the 'mother tree' idea
challenging.for: Marked carbon has moved between trees in a forest. In some tests, seedlings joined to a network survived better.
challenging.against: A 2023 review found very few forest studies that support it. The amounts of carbon were small, and several tests found no gain for seedlings.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that old trees pass food to young ones through fungi in the soil.

challenging.claim: A damaged plant sends out smells in order to warn neighbouring plants.
challenging.who: The usual way the finding is told
challenging.for: Neighbours do respond to the smells, and they are eaten less afterwards.
challenging.against: Helping a neighbour who competes for the same light and water gains the sender nothing. Many scientists think the smells are first a signal to the plant's own far leaves and to helpful wasps. Neighbours pick the news up, as you might overhear a call.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a plant's damage smell is meant for neighbouring plants.

challenging.claim: Pea seedlings can learn to link a breeze with light.
challenging.for: In her test, most trained seedlings grew towards the fan when no light was given.
challenging.against: In 2020 Kasey Markel repeated the test with more seedlings and measured without knowing which group each seedling was in. The effect did not appear.
challenging.context: This card is about a claim that pea plants can learn by linking two things, as a dog links a bell with food.

challenging.claim: Only a being with a brain can feel.
challenging.who: Many scientists who study brains and plants
challenging.for: In animals, feeling changes when the brain is hurt or put to sleep. No part of a plant looks like a brain.
challenging.against: Plants sense, signal, choose and keep information without a brain, and the gases that put animals to sleep work on plants as well. Nobody has shown that a brain is the only kind of body that can feel.
challenging.context: This card is about the common view that feeling needs a brain.

big_questions.q: A wasp, a neighbouring plant and you all receive the smell of a damaged leaf. Whom is that smell for?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the sender gains from each receiver.

big_questions.q: A seedling changes their growth for a week after a touch that lasted one second. What more would they have to do before you would say they remember?
big_questions.hint: Write your own test for remembering. Then check whether you pass it yourself when you ride a cycle.

big_questions.q: You cannot measure what your best friend feels. So how do you know she feels anything, and does your method work for a plant?
big_questions.hint: List the clues you use for your friend. Which of them does a plant give?

big_questions.q: A tree and a fungus are joined so closely that each would do badly alone. Is that two living beings or one?
big_questions.hint: Think about the bacteria in your own gut, which help you digest your food.

big_questions.q: A news story says 'trees talk to each other'. A scientist's paper says 'carbon moved between two trees'. Which one tells you more, and which would you rather read?
big_questions.hint: One is exciting and easy to remember. The other says exactly what was measured.

big_questions.q: If one careful scientist gets a result and another careful scientist does not, what should the rest of us believe in the meantime?
big_questions.hint: Think about the pea seedlings and the fan. Is 'we do not know yet' a proper answer?

story.title: The Wasps in the Maize
story.note: A made-up story. Gowri, her mother, Basavaraj Mama and Dr Nirmala are not real people. The science is real. The fall armyworm is a caterpillar that reached Karnataka in 2018 and feeds deep inside the rolled young leaves of maize. Maize chewed by caterpillars gives off a smell that a plain torn leaf does not, and small wasps follow that smell and lay their eggs in the caterpillars. Ted Turlings and his team showed this in 1990. A Krishi Vigyan Kendra is a government farm science centre. In real fields the wasps do not always win, and farmers often need other methods as well.
text: That July the maize stood as high as Gowri's waist. Her mother's two acres lay outside a village near Davanagere, where almost every field grew maize in the rains.
On Monday morning Amma came back from the field with a rolled-up leaf in her hand. She opened it on the veranda. The leaf was full of ragged holes. In its folds lay wet brown crumbs, like sawdust.
"The worm," said Amma.

Everyone in the village called them that. They were striped caterpillars, and when they were fully grown they were as long as Gowri's little finger. They lived deep inside the rolled young leaves at the top of each plant, where no bird could see them.

Basavaraj Mama from the next field was leaning on the gate. "Spray tomorrow, akka," he said. "I will bring my sprayer. One tank of the strong medicine, and every creeping thing in your field will be dead by evening."
Amma looked at the leaf for a long time. The spray cost money, and it made her cough for two days.
"First I want to know how bad it is," she said. "Gowri, walk the rows after school. Look at every tenth plant. Count how many have holes."

So that afternoon Gowri walked the rows with her maths notebook. She made a mark for each plant with holes and a dot for each plant without. By the fourth row she had noticed something that had nothing to do with counting.
Small black wasps were flying over some of the plants. They were no longer than a grain of rice. They hovered, landed and walked down into the rolled leaves. Over other plants there were none at all.
Gowri went back along the row and checked her marks. Every plant that had wasps overhead was a plant with holes.

Perhaps the wasps liked damaged leaves. Gowri knew where to find plenty of those. At the far corner, three days before, Shanthakka's goats had pushed through the thorn fence. They had torn up a whole patch before anyone chased them out. The leaves there hung in strips.
She stood in the torn patch and watched. There was not one wasp. She looked into the tops of the plants. There were no brown crumbs and no caterpillars.
Maybe the tears were too old. So Gowri chose a healthy plant, with no holes anywhere. She tore three of the leaves with her own fingers. Then she sat down on the bund to wait.
The shadows of the maize grew long. No wasp came to her plant. Two rows away, three wasps were circling a plant with fresh brown crumbs in the top.

Gowri thought about it all the way home. The caterpillars were hidden. She could find one only by unrolling a leaf. Yet the wasps found them from the air. A torn plant brought no wasps. A chewed plant brought them in.

Before school the next morning she unrolled the top leaf of one chewed plant. The caterpillar inside was limp and yellow, and hardly moved. Beside the caterpillar, stuck to the leaf, was a little heap of white cocoons, like grains of puffed rice.

When she came back to the house, Basavaraj Mama was at the gate with the sprayer on his back. A woman in a grey sari stood beside Amma, holding a file. Gowri had seen her before. She was Dr Nirmala from the Krishi Vigyan Kendra, and she had come to the village to talk about the worm.
"Mama, wait," said Gowri. "Come and see something first."

She led all three of them down the rows. She showed them the wasps over the chewed plants. She showed them the goat patch with no wasps, and her own torn plant with no wasps. Last she showed them the white cocoons.

"The wasps are hunting the worms," she said. "But they cannot see them, because the worms are inside. And it is not the holes they look for, or they would come to the goat patch. So something tells them which plants have worms. The only one who knows is the plant."
Basavaraj Mama laughed. "Now the maize is making phone calls."

"In a way, yes," said Dr Nirmala. She bent over the cocoons. "When a caterpillar chews, their spit gets into the wound. The maize senses the spit. Some hours later the plant gives off a smell that a torn leaf does not give. These wasps follow that smell. Each one lays her eggs inside a caterpillar. The young wasps eat the caterpillar and then spin these cocoons."
She looked at Gowri. "Scientists showed that only in 1990. You worked out half of it with three torn leaves."
"And if I spray?" asked Amma.
"The wasps fly in the open, so the spray reaches them first," said Dr Nirmala. "The caterpillar sits deep in the rolled leaf, where the spray hardly goes."
Nobody spoke for a moment. A wasp landed on the plant beside them and walked down out of sight.

"I cannot promise you the wasps will win," said Dr Nirmala. "Sometimes they do not. Count for four more days. Count the plants with fresh crumbs, and count the plants with cocoons. Then you will know which number is growing."
"Four days," said Amma to Basavaraj Mama. "Then I will decide."
Every evening that week Gowri walked the rows. Her notebook had two columns now. On Friday the cocoon column was longer than it had been on Tuesday, and the crumb column was shorter.
The wind came across the field. Gowri breathed in. To her it smelled only of green leaves. But the wasps were still arriving.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a maize plant can tell a caterpillar's bite from a plain tear, because the caterpillar's spit gets into the wound. Hours later the chewed plant gives off a mix of smell chemicals that a torn plant does not. Small wasps have receptors for that smell and follow it to the hidden caterpillar. So one living being's response to damage works as a signal for another. Gowri's test is a real control: she tore leaves herself, to check whether damage alone would bring the wasps.
ask: The caterpillars were hidden inside rolled leaves. What did Gowri notice that made her think the wasps were not using their eyes?
Why did Gowri tear three leaves on a healthy plant? What would it have meant if wasps had come to that plant?
The maize gave off the smell. The wasps followed it. Who gained from this, and how?
Dr Nirmala did not tell Amma what to do. She told her to count two things for four days. Why two things?
Gowri could not smell any difference between the plants. What does that tell you about the smells in the air around you now?

games.title: Which Path Did the News Take?
games.context: This is a card game about the four paths a plant's signals can take. Each card tells what happened. You choose the path the news took: inside the plant, through the air, through the soil from the roots, or along fungal threads. Then you turn the card to check.

printables.title: 20 news cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A caterpillar bites one leaf of a small plant. Two minutes later a far leaf of the same plant starts to switch on defences.
items.b: INSIDE. A wave of electric charge and calcium ran along the veins from the bitten leaf.

items.f: Caterpillars chew a maize plant. Some hours later, tiny wasps arrive from across the field and find the caterpillars.
items.b: AIR. The chewed plant gave off a smell, and the wasps followed that smell.

items.f: A witchweed seed has lain in a jowar field for three years. A jowar root grows close by, and the seed sprouts.
items.b: SOIL. The root let out a chemical into the soil, and the seed has receptors for that chemical.

items.f: A ghost plant is white and cannot make food. Yet they live on sugar that nearby trees made.
items.b: FUNGUS. The sugar reaches the ghost plant through a fungus that is joined to the trees' roots.

items.f: You touch the tip of a touch-me-not leaf. The leaflets fold pair after pair, all the way down the leaf.
items.b: INSIDE. An electrical signal runs along the leaf at 2 to 3 centimetres a second.

items.f: A ripe banana and a raw mango sit in a paper bag and do not touch. The mango ripens sooner than a mango kept alone.
items.b: AIR. The banana gives off the gas ethylene, and the mango responds to that gas.

items.f: A dodder seedling has no leaves and cannot make food. They bend and grow towards a tomato plant a few centimetres away.
items.b: AIR. The dodder seedling senses the smell of the tomato plant and grows towards it.

items.f: A ragi root is short of phosphorus. The threads of a helpful fungus nearby begin to branch towards the root.
items.b: SOIL. The root lets out a chemical into the soil that the fungus senses.

items.f: A pea plant is kept short of water. A neighbour sharing the same soil, with plenty of water, closes their leaf holes within an hour.
items.b: SOIL. The thirsty plant's roots let out a chemical, and the neighbour's roots sensed that chemical.

items.f: An orchid seed is as fine as dust and has no food store. Something brings food to the seed, and the seed starts to grow.
items.b: FUNGUS. A fungus grows into the seed and feeds the young orchid.

items.f: A plant's roots meet dry soil. Soon the tiny air holes in the leaves, far above, begin to close.
items.b: INSIDE. The roots send a hormone up to the leaves in the sap.

items.f: Someone clips the branches of a sagebrush bush. Wild tobacco plants growing beside the bush get their defences ready.
items.b: AIR. The clipped bush gave off damage smells, and the tobacco plants responded to them.

items.f: In a laboratory pot, fungal threads join two tomato plants. One catches a leaf disease, and the other switches on defence genes. A mesh that blocks the threads stops this.
items.b: FUNGUS. In this pot test the warning needed the fungal threads. Whether this happens in real fields is still being tested.

items.f: A fly touches one hair inside a Venus flytrap, and then a second hair. The two halves of the trap snap shut.
items.b: INSIDE. Each touch starts an electrical signal that crosses the trap.

items.f: A bean seedling's root lets out a chemical. Bacteria who can live inside bean roots swim towards the root.
items.b: SOIL. The bacteria sense the root's chemical in the soil water.

items.f: You tear a curry leaf in the kitchen. Someone in the next room calls out, 'Are you making sambar?'
items.b: AIR. Tearing the leaf let out smell chemicals, and they drifted to a nose in the next room.

items.f: The tip of a shoot senses light coming from one side. Lower down, the stem grows more on the shady side and bends.
items.b: INSIDE. A growth hormone moves down from the tip, more of it on the shady side.

items.f: One leaf of a bean plant is damaged. A second leaf of the same plant gets ready. It does not get ready when a plastic bag covers the first leaf.
items.b: AIR. The damaged leaf's smell reached the other leaf through the air, even though both are on one plant.

items.f: Scientists put marked phosphorus in soil that a plant's roots cannot reach. Later the marked phosphorus turns up in the plant's leaves.
items.b: FUNGUS. Fungal threads joined to the roots reached the phosphorus and carried it back.

items.f: Wind bends a young stem every day. Within half an hour, touch genes switch on, and over the next weeks the whole stem grows thicker.
items.b: INSIDE. Calcium ions flow into the bent cells, and the signal passes through the stem.

printables.title: 4 path tokens for each player (copy the set for every player)
items: INSIDE: through the plant's own body
AIR: as a smell or a gas
SOIL: as a chemical from the roots
FUNGUS: along fungal threads

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, news side up. Each player takes a set of four path tokens.
One player reads the top card aloud.
Each player chooses one token and lays it face down. On the count of three, everyone turns their token over.
Turn the card over and read the back. Every player with the right path scores one point.
A player who can also name the sender and the receiver scores one more point.
After 20 cards, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: try to reach 30 points out of 40. Then play again and try to beat your score.

setup.caption: 1. Put the cards in a pile. Each player takes four path tokens.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud while another child lays one token face down on the table.
setup.caption: 2. Read the card. Lay one token face down.

setup.art: Two tokens turned face up, one saying AIR and one saying SOIL, and the card turned over to show the answer AIR.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over, then turn the card to check.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Make a set of four path tokens for each player. 3. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, news side up.
flow.say: Each card tells some news that reached a receiver. We will work out which path the news took.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Make four tokens for each player. Shuffle the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Path Did the News Take? Here you set up the cards and the path tokens.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Everyone lays a token face down. 3. Count to three and turn the tokens over. 4. Turn the card and read the back.
flow.say: Ask two questions each time. Is the receiver part of the same plant? If not, is the receiver above the ground or below it?
flow.kid: Read the card. Is the receiver the same plant? Above ground or below? Choose your token.

ask.q: A leaf warns another leaf of the same plant through the air. Why might that be quicker than going inside?
good: The two leaves may be close in the air but far apart along the stem.
A smell crosses a small gap in seconds.

flow.parent: The two questions sort most cards. News to the same plant usually goes inside. News above the ground goes through the air. Below the ground, the card says whether a fungus was the carrier.
flow.context: This is the main part of Which Path Did the News Take? Here you read each card and choose a path token.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Sort the 20 cards into four heaps by path. 3. Ask your child which heap holds the results that scientists are least sure of.
flow.say: Which cards surprised us? Which heap has a result that is still being tested?
flow.kid: Count your points. Sort the cards into four heaps. Which heap is least certain?

check.q: A chewed maize plant gives off a smell, and wasps follow it to the caterpillar. Which path did the news take?
check.why: The wasps are not part of the plant, and they are above the ground. So the news reached them through the air as a smell. Choosing 'inside the plant' usually means thinking only of the plant's own far leaves, which get news that way.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Path Did the News Take? Here you count the points and sort the cards by path.

games.title: Under the Forest: can six trees last eight rounds?
games.context: This is a board game about a debated idea. Suzanne Simard thinks big trees pass sugar through fungal threads to seedlings in deep shade. Other scientists doubt that this matters in real forests. Here you play the forest three ways, with dried beans as sugar, and compare.

printables.title: The forest board, drawn on a sheet of paper
items: Draw six circles in a ring, each big enough to hold ten beans.
Going round the ring, name the circles A, E, C, B, F and D.
A and B are big trees in full sun. Write 'makes 3, uses 2' in each.
C and D are middle trees. Write 'makes 2, uses 1' in each.
E and F are seedlings in deep shade. Write 'makes 0, uses 1' in each.
Draw a line from each circle to the circle on either side. These six lines are the fungal threads.
Draw one small bowl in the middle of the ring and write 'fungus' in it.

printables.title: Score sheet for the three forests
items: Forest 1, no sharing: trees alive after 8 rounds: __ out of 6
Forest 2, sharing along the threads: trees alive after 8 rounds: __ out of 6
Forest 2: beans in the fungus bowl at the end: __
Forest 3, seedlings in light shade and no sharing: trees alive after 8 rounds: __ out of 6
In which forest did the threads change who lived? __

rules: You need the board, about 40 dried beans such as rajma or chana, a die and a coin for each tree that dies. Put 3 beans on every tree. The rest are the bank.
Each round has four parts: roll, make, share and live.
Roll the die. On 1, caterpillars strip tree A. On 2 they strip B, on 3 they strip C, and on 4 they strip D. A stripped tree makes no sugar this round. On 5 or 6, nothing happens.
Make: every tree that was not stripped takes from the bank the beans that tree makes.
Share: you may move beans from one tree to the next tree along a line. Each time you move beans along one line, put 1 of those beans in the fungus bowl.
Live: every tree pays back to the bank the beans that tree uses. A tree that cannot pay dies. Put a coin on that circle. A dead tree makes nothing, but beans can still pass through the circle.
The game ends after 8 rounds. Your score is the number of trees still alive. Everyone plays together as one team.
Forest 1: play with no sharing at all. Forest 2: play again with sharing. Forest 3: the seedlings stand in light shade and make 1 bean each. Play with no sharing.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with six circles drawn in a ring, labelled A, E, C, B, F and D, joined by lines, with three dried beans in each circle and a small bowl drawn in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Draw six trees in a ring and join them. Put 3 beans on each.

setup.art: A hand rolling a die beside the board, and another hand taking three beans from a heap and putting them on circle A.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the die. Trees that were not stripped take the beans they make.

setup.art: A hand moving three beans along a line from circle A to circle E, with one bean dropped into the bowl in the middle.
setup.caption: 3. Share along a line. One bean from each move goes to the fungus.

setup.art: The board with a coin lying on circle F and beans in the other five circles.
setup.caption: 4. All trees pay the beans they use. A tree that cannot pay dies.

flow.do: 1. Draw the board as the printable says. 2. Count out about 40 beans. 3. Put 3 beans on each tree. 4. Read the four parts of a round aloud.
flow.say: Each bean is sugar that a tree made from light. The seedlings stand in deep shade, so they make none. What do you think will happen to them?
flow.kid: Draw the board. Put 3 beans on each tree. Read the four parts of a round.
flow.context: This is the first step of Under the Forest. Here you draw the board and set out the beans.

flow.do: 1. Play Forest 1 for 8 rounds with no sharing. 2. Put a coin on each tree that dies. 3. Write the number of living trees on the score sheet.
flow.say: In this forest no tree is joined to another. Roll, make and live. Watch the seedlings.
flow.kid: Play 8 rounds with no sharing. Put a coin on each dead tree. Write the score.
flow.parent: Both seedlings die in round 4, because each starts with 3 beans and uses 1 a round. A big tree stripped twice in a row early in the game can die too.
flow.context: This step of Under the Forest is the first game. Here the trees do not share at all.

flow.do: 1. Set the board up again with 3 beans on each tree. 2. Play Forest 2 for 8 rounds, with sharing. 3. Count the living trees and the beans in the fungus bowl.
flow.say: Now the fungal threads carry sugar. Every move costs one bean. Is it better to send a seedling one bean each round, or several at once?
flow.kid: Set up again. Play 8 rounds with sharing. Each move costs one bean. Count the trees left.

ask.q: Why is it better to send three beans in one move than one bean in three moves?
good: Each move costs one bean for the fungus.
Three single moves would lose all three beans. One move of three loses only one.

ask.q: What did the fungus gain in this forest?
good: A bean from every move.
The more the trees share, the more the fungus gets.

flow.parent: All six trees can live through 8 rounds if the big and middle trees send beans to the seedlings in moves of three or four. If a tree is lost, play again.
flow.context: This step of Under the Forest is the second game. Here the trees share sugar along the fungal threads.

flow.do: 1. Set up again. This time each seedling makes 1 bean a round. 2. Play Forest 3 for 8 rounds with no sharing. 3. Compare the three scores.
flow.say: Now the seedlings get a little light. Do they need the threads? What would a scientist have to measure in a real forest to know which game is true?
flow.kid: Set up again. Seedlings now make 1 bean. Play 8 rounds with no sharing. Compare all three scores.

ask.q: What would a scientist need to measure to find out which forest is the real one?
good: How much food a shaded seedling makes for themself.
How much sugar really arrives through the threads.
Whether seedlings cut off from the threads die more often.

check.q: In the game, sharing saved the seedlings in deep shade. What does that show about real forests?
options: Real trees feed seedlings in the same way
What would happen if the idea is true
check.why: A game follows the rules we give it. It shows what the idea would lead to, but it cannot show that the idea is true. Only measurements in a real forest can do that. Choosing the first answer usually means treating a model as evidence.

flow.context: This is the last step of Under the Forest. Here the seedlings make a little food themselves, and you compare the three games.

experiments.title: The Touch Test: does a daily stroke change how moong seedlings grow?
experiments.context: In this experiment you grow two cups of moong seedlings at the same window. You stroke the seedlings in one cup twice a day for six days, and you never touch the seedlings in the other cup. Then you measure both cups.
experiments.question: If seedlings are stroked for a few seconds twice a day, do they grow differently from seedlings that nobody touches?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After six days of strokes, which cup will have the taller seedlings: the stroked cup, the untouched cup, or neither? Will the stems look or feel different? Write your guess and your reason for it.
experiments.fair_test: Change only one thing: the strokes. Use seeds from one packet, two cups of the same kind, the same soil and the same amount of water. Keep both cups at the same window and swap their places every day, so that both get the same light. Keep 10 seedlings in each cup, because one seedling can be a fluke. The untouched cup is the control.
results_table: How the stems look and feel

a ruler marked in centimetres
a tablespoon, a marker pen and a notebook

setup.caption: 1. Plant 12 soaked moong seeds in each of two cups. Mark them S and U.

setup.caption: 2. On day 5, keep 10 shoots in each cup and measure every one.
