flow.do: 1. Count out 30 whole green moong seeds. 2. Put them in a katori and cover them with water. 3. Leave them overnight.
flow.say: We are going to find out whether a plant responds to being stroked. First the seeds need a night in water, so that they start to grow.
flow.kid: Count 30 moong seeds. Cover them with water. Leave them overnight.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Touch Test. Here you soak the moong seeds.

flow.do: 1. Poke three small holes in the bottom of each paper cup. 2. Fill both cups with damp soil to two finger-widths below the rim. 3. Push 12 seeds into each cup, one finger-joint deep and well spread out. 4. Mark one cup S for stroked and the other U for untouched. 5. Stand both cups on a plate at a bright window.
flow.say: The two cups must be the same in every way we can manage. Each cup gets two tablespoons of water every day.
flow.kid: Fill two cups with damp soil. Plant 12 seeds in each. Mark them S and U. Stand both at a bright window.
flow.parent: Steel tumblers have no holes, so give them only one tablespoon of water a day. Twelve seeds are planted because a few may not come up. Shoots usually show within 2 days. In cold weather they take longer.
flow.context: This step of the Touch Test is for planting. Here you plant the soaked seeds in two cups that are the same.

flow.do: 1. Pull out the smallest shoots until each cup has 10. 2. Ask your child for a guess and a reason, and write both down. 3. Measure each shoot from the soil to the top. 4. Find the mean height for each cup. 5. Sweep the card gently across the tops in cup S, 20 times.
flow.say: Before the first stroke, what do you think the strokes will do? Why do you think so? The shoots should bend about halfway over and spring back.
flow.kid: Keep 10 shoots in each cup. Guess, and say why. Measure every shoot. Stroke cup S 20 times with the card.
flow.wait: Do this on day 5, or when most shoots are 3 to 4 centimetres tall

ask.q: Why do we measure both cups before the first stroke?
good: So that we know whether the cups were the same at the start.
Then we can compare how much each cup grew.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Common guesses are that touching will harm the shoots, or that it will make no difference. To find a mean, add the ten heights and divide by 10.
flow.context: This step of the Touch Test is for the guess, the first measurements and the first strokes.

flow.do: 1. Every morning and every evening, sweep the card across the tops in cup S 20 times. 2. Never touch the shoots in cup U. 3. Give both cups the same water. 4. Swap the places of the two cups once a day.
flow.say: Twenty sweeps take about half a minute. Be gentle. The shoots should bend and spring back, and none should snap.
flow.kid: Stroke cup S 20 times, morning and evening. Do not touch cup U. Water both. Swap their places.
flow.parent: If you miss one session, carry on. If a shoot snaps, take that shoot out, and take the smallest shoot out of the other cup too. After two or three days the leaves open, and the card brushes the leaves.
flow.think: After two days, look at both cups without measuring. Can you see any difference yet?
flow.context: This step of the Touch Test lasts five days. Here you stroke the seedlings in cup S twice a day.

flow.do: 1. Cover the letters S and U with a strip of paper. 2. Ask someone who does not know which cup is which to measure every shoot. 3. Find the mean for each cup. 4. Bend one shoot in each cup gently with a finger, and compare how stiff the stems feel. 5. Draw the bar chart.
flow.say: The person who measures should not know which cup was stroked. Why do you think scientists take that trouble?
flow.kid: Cover the letters. Ask someone else to measure every shoot. Find both means. Feel one stem from each cup. Draw two bars.

ask.q: Why should the person who measures not know which cup was stroked?
good: Someone who expects one cup to be shorter may measure it a little shorter without meaning to.
Then the result does not depend on what we hoped to find.

flow.parent: If nobody else is at home, your child can measure with the letters covered and the cups swapped about. Stroked shoots are often 1 to 3 centimetres shorter on average, and their stems feel stiffer. Single shoots overlap, so compare the means.
flow.context: This step of the Touch Test is for the last measurements. Here someone measures both cups without knowing which is which.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for three sentences: what they thought, what they saw, and why it may have happened. 2. Ask what else, besides the strokes, could have made a difference. 3. Only then read the explanation 'How a touch changes the way a plant grows' together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Was anything different between the cups apart from the strokes?
flow.kid: Say what you thought. Say what you saw. Say why it may have happened. Was the test fair?

ask.q: Each stroke lasted about a second, but the difference took days to show. What does that tell you?
good: The seedlings went on responding long after each touch ended.
The response was a change in growth, and growth takes days.

ask.q: Where might a wild plant get bent many times a day?
good: In a windy place.
Where animals brush past.

flow.parent: If the two means differ by less than half a centimetre, say so plainly. That is a real result. The strokes may have been too gentle, or six days may be too few. Your child can run the test for four more days.

check.q: In the Touch Test, why was one cup of seedlings never stroked?
options: To have something to compare with
check.why: The untouched cup is the control. Both cups had the same seeds, soil, water and light, so a difference at the end comes from the strokes. Without the control, you could not tell whether the stroked seedlings were shorter than they would have been anyway.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Touch Test. Here you explain your result and check whether the test was fair.

experiments.title: The Drop Test: does a touch-me-not stop folding for a harmless drop? (if you can get a touch-me-not)
experiments.context: In this experiment you repeat a well-known test from 2014. You drop a potted touch-me-not a short way on to a soft towel, many times, and watch whether the leaves go on folding. You need a touch-me-not plant in a small pot.
experiments.question: If a touch-me-not is dropped gently again and again and comes to no harm, do the leaves go on folding every time? If they stop, is the plant simply tired?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After 60 gentle drops, will the leaves still fold as fully as after the first drop? Then guess again. If you shake the plant sideways straight afterwards, will the leaves fold? Write both guesses and your reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Drop the pot from the same height every time, 15 centimetres, on to the same folded towel. Leave the same time between drops, about 10 seconds. Watch the same three leaves and score them in the same way each time. The sideways shake is the control for tiredness, because it tests whether the plant can still fold.

materials.item: a touch-me-not plant in a small, light plastic pot
a bath towel, folded in four
a ruler
short pieces of coloured thread
a watch or phone that shows seconds
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A touch-me-not has small thorns on the stems, so hold the pot and not the plant.

schedule.what: Drop the pot 60 times and score three leaves. Shake the pot sideways, score again and draw the graph.
Drop the pot once and score the leaves. Compare with the first drop of day 1.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for drops 1, 20, 40 and 60, for the shake, and for the one drop on day 2. Draw a line graph of the total score against the number of drops. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: fold score of three leaves during 60 drops
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished graph can look like. Your plant may do something different.

setup.art: A small potted touch-me-not with open leaves, three of them marked by bits of coloured thread tied to the stem beside them, and a bath towel folded in four on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Mark three leaves with thread. Fold a towel in four on the floor.

setup.art: Two hands holding the pot upright above the towel, with a ruler standing beside it showing a gap of 15 centimetres under the pot.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the pot 15 centimetres above the towel and let go. Do this 60 times.

setup.art: A child looking closely at one marked leaf and writing 0, 1 or 2 in a table in a notebook.
setup.caption: 3. Score each marked leaf: 0 for open, 1 for half folded, 2 for fully folded.

setup.art: Two hands shaking the pot from side to side, with the leaves of the plant folding.
setup.caption: 4. After the last drop, shake the pot sideways and score again.

flow.do: 1. An hour ahead, tie a loose thread to the stem beside each of three leaves. 2. Leave the plant in bright shade until all the leaves are open. 3. Fold the towel in four and lay it on the floor. 4. Ask for both guesses and the reasons, and write them down.
flow.say: We will score three leaves. An open leaf scores 0, a half-folded leaf 1 and a fully folded leaf 2. What do you think will happen after many drops? Why?
flow.kid: Mark three leaves with thread. Wait until they are open. Fold the towel. Guess what will happen, and say why.
flow.parent: Tying the threads makes the leaves fold, so do it an hour ahead. Press the soil down firmly so that none spills.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Drop Test. Here you mark three leaves and make your guesses.

flow.do: 1. Hold the pot upright with the base 15 centimetres above the towel, and let go. 2. Five seconds later, score the three leaves. 3. Drop the pot again every 10 seconds, until you have done 60 drops. 4. Score the leaves after drops 20, 40 and 60.
flow.say: Count the drops aloud. Keep the height the same every time. Watch whether the leaves begin to open again while the drops go on.
flow.kid: Drop the pot 15 cm on to the towel. Score the leaves. Do 60 drops, one every 10 seconds. Score after drops 20, 40 and 60.
flow.parent: Keep one hand near the pot so that it cannot tip over. One person drops and counts, and the other watches the leaves. If the leaves are still fully folded after 60 drops, write that down. It is a real result.
flow.context: This is the main part of the Drop Test. Here you drop the pot 60 times and score the leaves.

flow.do: 1. Straight after drop 60, hold the pot and shake it from side to side for five seconds. 2. Score the three leaves. 3. Ask what this shows about tiredness.
flow.say: This is the test for tiredness. If the plant was too tired to fold, what should happen now? What does happen?
flow.kid: Shake the pot sideways for five seconds. Score the leaves. Was the plant too tired to fold?

ask.q: Suppose the leaves fold for the shake but not for the drop. Can 'the plant is tired' explain that?
good: No. A tired plant could not fold for the shake either.
The plant still had the energy to fold, and had stopped only for the drop.

flow.context: This step of the Drop Test is the control. Here you shake the plant to find out whether the leaves can still fold.

flow.do: 1. Draw a line graph of the total score after drops 1, 20, 40 and 60. 2. Mark the score after the shake as a separate point. 3. Ask your child for three sentences: what they thought, what they saw, and why. 4. Then read the explanation 'Can a plant learn?' together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Does your graph go down, stay level or go up?
flow.kid: Draw the graph. Mark the shake as its own point. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: In the 2014 experiment the plants opened their leaves again before the 60 drops were over, and folded at once for a shake. Home results vary with the plant, the light and the landing. Your child reports what your plant did.
flow.context: This step of the Drop Test is for the graph and for explaining the result.

flow.do: 1. Leave the plant untouched at a bright window until the next day. 2. Drop the pot once from 15 centimetres and score the leaves. 3. Then touch one leaf with a finger and score it. 4. Compare with yesterday's first drop.
flow.say: Yesterday's first drop scored high. If today's first drop scores low, what has the plant kept from yesterday?
flow.kid: Next day, drop the pot once. Score the leaves. Touch one leaf and score it. Compare with yesterday.
flow.parent: In the 2014 experiment many plants still did not fold for a drop a month later. A plant kept in strong sunlight may go back to folding sooner.

check.q: A touch-me-not stops folding after many harmless drops, but folds at once when shaken. What does the shake show?
options: The plant was too tired to fold
The drops had damaged the leaves
check.why: The leaves folded for the shake, so the plant still had the energy and the working parts to fold. That rules out tiredness and damage. The plant had stopped responding only to the harmless drop. Choosing 'tired' is the first idea most people have, and the shake is the test that checks it.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Drop Test. Here you test the plant again a day later.

activities.title: The Torn Leaf Test: can your nose tell a damaged leaf from a whole one?
activities.context: In this activity one katori holds whole leaves and another holds torn leaves of the same kind. With your eyes closed, you find out whether your nose can tell which is which, and from how far away.

materials.item: fresh leaves of one kind. Curry leaves, tulsi, mint, coriander or methi are easiest. Palak, cabbage or grass also work from close up.
katoris or tumblers of the same kind
a ruler or a measuring tape
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Write how many times out of 5 you chose the torn katori. Write the greatest distance at which you could smell the torn leaves. Draw the test, and label the sender, the carrier and the receiver.

setup.art: Two steel katoris on a table, each holding three whole curry leaves.
setup.caption: 1. Put three whole leaves in each of two katoris. Smell both.

setup.art: A grown-up tearing the leaves in one katori into pieces while a child sits with eyes closed.
setup.caption: 2. With your eyes closed, let someone tear the leaves in one katori.

setup.art: A child with eyes closed sniffing above a katori held a hand-width under the nose.
setup.caption: 3. Smell each katori and say which has the torn leaves. Do this five times.

setup.art: A child standing with eyes closed while a grown-up holds the torn katori at arm's length and a measuring tape runs between them.
setup.caption: 4. Find how far away you can first smell the torn leaves.

flow.do: 1. Put three whole leaves in each of two katoris. 2. Your child smells both from a hand-width above. 3. Ask whether tearing the leaves in one katori will change its smell, and why.
flow.say: Both katoris smell the same now. I am going to tear the leaves in one. Will your nose know which one, with your eyes closed? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Smell both katoris. Will tearing the leaves change the smell? Guess, and say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Torn Leaf Test. Here you smell whole leaves and make a guess.

flow.do: 1. Your child closes their eyes. 2. Tear each leaf in one katori into four pieces. 3. Swap the katoris about. 4. Hold each in turn a hand-width under your child's nose, and ask which is torn. 5. Do this five times, and write down each answer.
flow.say: Keep your eyes closed. Which katori has the torn leaves? I will tell you how many you got right at the end.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Smell each katori. Say which has the torn leaves. Do it five times.
flow.parent: With curry leaves or tulsi, most children are right five times out of five. Palak and grass smell weaker, so hold the katori closer. A child with a blocked nose can swap jobs with you.
flow.context: This is the main part of the Torn Leaf Test. Here you try five times to pick the torn leaves by smell alone.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands two big steps away, with eyes closed. 2. Bring the torn katori closer, one hand-width at a time. 3. Your child says 'now' at the first smell. 4. Measure from the katori to your child's nose.
flow.say: The smell is spreading out through the air. Who else, besides you, could receive it? What might each of them do?
flow.kid: Stand two steps away, eyes closed. Say 'now' when you smell the leaves. Measure how far away they are.

ask.q: A torn leaf smells different from a whole leaf. Who could make use of that news?
good: An insect that eats leaves, or an insect that hunts leaf-eaters.
Another plant nearby.
A person who is cooking.

check.q: With eyes closed, you pick the torn leaves five times out of five. What does that show?
options: Torn leaves give off something whole leaves do not
Leaves smell only when someone is near
check.why: Five right answers in a row would happen by luck only about once in 32 tries. So your nose was receiving something real. Tearing let out smell chemicals that were stored in the leaf, or made the leaf produce new ones. 'Lucky' is a fair answer after one or two tries, which is why you did five.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Torn Leaf Test. Here you measure how far the smell of the torn leaves travels.

activities.title: See the Threads: what is the body of a fungus made of?
activities.context: In this activity a mould grows on a piece of chapati inside a sealed bag. Through the bag, with a magnifying glass, you look at the fine threads that make up the body of a fungus.

materials.item: half a chapati, an idli or a slice of bakery bread
a clear zip bag, or a clear plastic box with a lid
sticky tape and a marker pen
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera on full zoom
a ruler and a notebook

activities.safety: Do not open the bag once it is sealed. Mould gives off a fine dust of spores, and breathing spores can make some people cough or wheeze. On the last day, put the sealed bag in the dustbin.

schedule.what: Seal a damp piece of chapati in a clear bag and put it in a warm, dim place.
Look through the bag for white fluff. Draw round the patch on the outside of the bag.
Look at the threads through a magnifying glass, draw them and measure how far they have spread.

activities.record: Draw what you see through the magnifying glass on day 5: the threads, and any dark dots on stalks. Write how far the patch spread between day 3 and day 5.

setup.art: A piece of chapati with a few drops of water on it being slid into a clear zip bag.
setup.caption: 1. Wipe a piece of chapati on a shelf, add five drops of water and seal it in a clear bag.

setup.art: A sealed clear bag with a white fluffy patch on the chapati inside, and a marker line drawn round the patch on the outside of the bag.
setup.caption: 2. On day 3, draw round the white fluff on the outside of the bag.

setup.art: A child holding a magnifying glass against the sealed bag and looking at fine white threads with tiny dark dots on stalks.
setup.caption: 3. On day 5, look at the threads through a magnifying glass. Keep the bag sealed.

flow.do: 1. Wipe the piece of chapati across a shelf or a windowsill. 2. Sprinkle five drops of water on it. 3. Seal it in the clear bag and tape the opening shut. 4. Put the bag in a warm, dim place, such as a kitchen shelf.
flow.say: Fungus spores are in the dust all around us. We are giving some of them food and water. What do you think we will see in five days?
flow.kid: Wipe the chapati on a shelf. Add five drops of water. Seal the bag and tape it shut.
flow.parent: Packaged bread has chemicals that slow mould, so it can take ten days. A chapati, an idli or bakery bread is faster.
flow.context: This is the first step of See the Threads. Here you seal a damp piece of chapati in a clear bag.

flow.do: 1. Look through the bag without opening it. 2. Find any white, fluffy patch. 3. Draw round the patch on the outside of the bag with the marker.
flow.say: Is anything growing? Where did it begin? Mark the edge, so that we can see how far it spreads.
flow.kid: Look through the bag. Do not open it. Find the white fluff. Draw round it.
flow.context: This step of See the Threads is on day 3. Here you mark how far the mould has spread.

flow.do: 1. Hold the magnifying glass against the bag, over the edge of the fluffy patch. 2. Your child looks for single threads and draws them. 3. Look for tiny dark dots on stalks. 4. Measure how far the patch has spread past the marker line. 5. Put the sealed bag in the dustbin.
flow.say: Each thread is one hypha. The whole patch is one mycelium, and the dark dots hold spores. How is this body different from a plant's body?
flow.kid: Look through the magnifying glass. Find single threads and draw them. Measure how far they spread. Bin the sealed bag.

ask.q: The threads are thinner than a hair. How would that help a fungus who lives in soil?
good: Thin threads can get into gaps too small for a root.
A lot of thin thread touches a lot of soil.

flow.parent: This mould is a decomposer, who feeds on dead food. The fungi joined to plant roots are different kinds, but their bodies are built from the same sort of threads.

check.q: What is the main body of a fungus made of?
check.why: The body is a web of fine threads, called the mycelium. A mushroom is only the part that makes spores, as a mango is the fruit and not the whole tree. Choosing 'mushroom' is common, because the mushroom is the only part we usually see.

flow.context: This is the last step of See the Threads. Here you look at the threads of the mould through a magnifying glass.

activities.title: How Fast Is the News? Three signal speeds on a ruler
activities.context: In this activity you move a finger along a ruler at the speed of three signals. They are the warning wave inside a small plant, the signal in a touch-me-not leaf, and a signal in your own nerves.

materials.item: a 30 centimetre ruler
a watch or phone that shows seconds
a coin
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Make a table with three rows: the warning wave in a small plant, the signal in a touch-me-not leaf, and a nerve signal. For each, write the speed and the time it takes to travel 30 centimetres.

setup.art: A child's fingertip resting on the zero mark of a ruler on a table, beside a phone showing a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 1. Move a fingertip 1 millimetre each second for 30 seconds.

setup.art: A child sliding a coin along a 30 centimetre ruler while watching a stopwatch that shows 10 seconds.
setup.caption: 2. Slide a coin the whole length of the ruler in 10 seconds.

flow.do: 1. Lay the ruler on a table. 2. Your child puts a fingertip on 0. 3. Count seconds aloud together, and your child moves the fingertip 1 millimetre at each count, up to 30.
flow.say: This is the speed of the warning wave in a small plant after a caterpillar's bite. Before we start, how far will you get in 30 seconds?
flow.kid: Put a finger on 0. Move 1 millimetre each second. Count to 30. How far did you get?
flow.parent: The fingertip reaches 3 centimetres. Moving this slowly feels strange, and that is the point.
flow.context: This is the first step of How Fast Is the News? Here your finger moves at the speed of a plant's warning wave.

flow.do: 1. Your child slides a coin from 0 to 30 centimetres in 10 seconds. 2. Work out the speed together: 3 centimetres each second. 3. Ask how many times faster this is than the first signal.
flow.say: This is the speed of the signal that folds a touch-me-not leaf. How many times faster is it than the warning wave?
flow.kid: Slide a coin from 0 to 30 cm in 10 seconds. How many times faster is this?

ask.q: 3 centimetres a second is how many times as fast as 1 millimetre a second?
good: 30 times, because 3 centimetres is 30 millimetres.

flow.context: This step of How Fast Is the News? shows the speed of the signal in a touch-me-not leaf.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that a fast nerve signal travels 100 metres each second. 2. Work out together how long it would take to cross the ruler. 3. Ask whether the plant's wave is too slow to be useful.
flow.say: Your fastest nerves would cross this ruler in three thousandths of a second. A caterpillar needs many minutes to eat one leaf. So is the plant's wave fast enough?
flow.kid: A nerve signal crosses the ruler in a blink. A caterpillar eats slowly. Is the plant's wave fast enough?

check.q: A plant's warning wave moves about 1 millimetre a second. Why is that fast enough?
options: Caterpillars eat far more slowly than that
check.why: The wave reaches leaves a few centimetres away in a minute or two. A caterpillar takes many minutes to finish one leaf and move on. So the far leaves have time to make bitter chemicals. A signal only has to be faster than the danger.

flow.context: This is the last step of How Fast Is the News? Here you compare the plant's signals with a signal in your nerves.

activities.title: Stroke a Tendril (if you have a gourd, pea or grape climber nearby)
activities.context: In this activity you stroke one side of a young tendril with a matchstick and watch what the tendril does. A tendril is the thin curling thread that a climbing plant uses to hold on. You need a climber with tendrils, in a garden, a park or a balcony pot.

materials.item: a climbing plant with young tendrils, such as bitter gourd, ridge gourd, bottle gourd, cucumber, pumpkin, pea, passion fruit or grape
a matchstick or a thin twig
a few drops of water
a watch, a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Draw each of the three tendrils at the start, after 5 minutes and after 30 minutes. Write which way the stroked tendril curled.

setup.art: A bitter gourd vine on a balcony trellis with three young straight tendrils reaching out into the air, each marked with a small numbered paper tag on the stem nearby.
setup.caption: 1. Find three young, straight tendrils that are not touching anything.

setup.art: A child stroking the underside of the tip of one tendril with a matchstick.
setup.caption: 2. Stroke one side of the first tendril ten times. Put drops of water on the second. Leave the third alone.

setup.art: The stroked tendril curled into a hook, the wet tendril and the untouched tendril still straight.
setup.caption: 3. Look again after 5 minutes and after 30 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Find three young, straight tendrils that are not touching anything. 2. Draw all three. 3. Ask what a tendril will do if one side is stroked, and why. 4. Ask the same about a drop of water.
flow.say: A tendril has to find something to hold. What do you think this one will do if a stick strokes one side? And what if a raindrop lands on one? Why?
flow.kid: Find three straight young tendrils. Draw them. Guess what a stroke will do. Guess what a water drop will do.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stroke a Tendril. Here you choose three tendrils and make two guesses.

flow.do: 1. Stroke one side of the first tendril, near the tip, ten times with the matchstick. 2. Let five drops of water fall on the second tendril. 3. Leave the third tendril alone as the control. 4. Look at all three once a minute for five minutes, and draw them.
flow.say: Watch closely. Is anything changing? Which way is the stroked tendril bending: towards the side you stroked, or away from it?
flow.kid: Stroke the first tendril ten times. Drip water on the second. Leave the third. Look every minute and draw.
flow.parent: A young gourd tendril often starts to curl within 2 to 10 minutes, towards the stroked side. Old tendrils and coiled tendrils do not respond. Charles Darwin wrote in 1875 that his tendrils curled for a thread but took no notice of drops of water. See what yours do.
flow.context: This is the main part of Stroke a Tendril. Here you stroke one tendril, wet another and leave the third alone.

flow.do: 1. Come back after 30 minutes. 2. Draw the three tendrils again. 3. Ask why it might help a climber to respond to a stick but not to rain.
flow.say: Compare the three. Why might it help a climbing plant to curl for a stick and not for a raindrop?
flow.kid: Come back after 30 minutes. Draw the three tendrils. Why curl for a stick, but not for rain?

check.q: A tendril curls round a stick that rubs one side. Why is curling towards the rubbed side useful?
options: The rubbed side is where the support is
check.why: Something that keeps rubbing one side is probably a twig or a wire the plant can hold. Curling towards that side wraps the tendril round it. Choosing 'hurt' treats the touch as damage, but the stroke is gentle and the tendril stays healthy.

flow.context: This is the last step of Stroke a Tendril. Here you compare the three tendrils after half an hour.

activities.title: Learned or Tired? Work out what an experiment showed
activities.context: This activity is about a real experiment from 2014. Touch-me-not plants were dropped gently 60 times, and by the end they had stopped folding their leaves. You work out which later results fit the idea 'the plants were tired' and which fit 'the plants had learned'.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.record: Keep your table. It has three rows, one for each result, and a tick under 'tired', 'learned' or both. Under it, write one more test you would do.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a table of two columns headed 'tired' and 'learned' and three empty rows.
setup.caption: 1. Draw two columns: 'tired' and 'learned'.

setup.art: A child ticking the 'learned' column beside a small drawing of a pot being shaken sideways with the plant's leaves folded.
setup.caption: 2. For each result, tick the explanation that fits.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child what happened: plants were dropped 15 centimetres on to foam, 60 times, and stopped folding. 2. Ask for two different explanations. 3. Write 'tired' and 'learned' at the top of two columns.
flow.say: The plants folded at first and then stopped. Give me two different reasons why that could happen.
flow.kid: Plants were dropped 60 times and stopped folding. Think of two reasons why. Draw two columns.
flow.parent: Your child may offer other ideas, such as 'the leaves were damaged'. Add a column for any idea that can be tested.
flow.context: This is the first step of Learned or Tired? Here you think of two explanations for one result.

flow.do: 1. Result one: straight after the drops, the plants were shaken sideways, and they folded at once. 2. Result two: after six days of rest, the plants were dropped again, and they stayed open. 3. Result three: plants kept in dim light stopped folding sooner than plants kept in bright light. 4. For each result, ask which explanation fits, and tick that column.
flow.say: For each result, ask what a tired plant would do and what a plant who had learned would do. Then see which one happened.
flow.kid: One: shaken sideways, the plants folded. Two: six days later, they stayed open for a drop. Three: plants in dim light stopped sooner. Tick what fits.

good: Result one. A tired plant could not fold for the shake.
Result two. Six days of rest would cure tiredness, but the plants still stayed open.

flow.parent: Results one and two fit 'learned' and not 'tired'. Result three fits both. A plant in dim light has less energy, so they might tire sooner. But folding also costs such a plant more light, so they gain more by learning fast. A result that fits both ideas does not tell us which idea is right.
flow.context: This is the main part of Learned or Tired? Here you check three real results against two explanations.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what else a doubting scientist might say. 2. Ask what test would answer that doubt. 3. Write the test under the table.
flow.say: Some scientists still doubt that this is learning. What might they say? What test would you do to answer them?
flow.kid: What might a doubting scientist say? What test would answer the doubt? Write it down.
flow.parent: Good answers: do it again with more plants, in another laboratory, with a person who scores the leaves without knowing which plants were trained.

check.q: Trained touch-me-nots fold for a shake but not for a drop. Which explanation does this rule out?
options: The plants were too tired to fold
The plants learned the drop was harmless
The plants can sense a shake
check.why: A plant too tired to fold would not fold for the shake either. So tiredness is ruled out. The result fits the idea that the plants had stopped responding to the drop alone. Ruling out an explanation is different from proving the other one, which is why scientists go on testing.

flow.context: This is the last step of Learned or Tired? Here you think of one more test a doubting scientist would ask for.

activities.title: Three Chairs: do plants feel?
activities.context: This activity is a short debate about a question that scientists have not settled. Three chairs stand for three views. You sit in each chair in turn and argue for that view, using evidence from this unit.

materials.item: chairs or cushions
slips of paper and a pencil

activities.record: Write which chair you chose at the end, and the one piece of evidence that mattered most to you. Write what new evidence could make you move to another chair.

setup.art: Three chairs in a row with paper labels reading 'Yes, plants feel', 'These are responses, and feeling needs a brain' and 'Nobody can test this yet'.
setup.caption: 1. Label three chairs with the three views.

setup.art: A child sitting in the middle chair holding a slip of paper and speaking, while a grown-up sits in the first chair listening.
setup.caption: 2. Sit in each chair for two minutes and argue for that view with evidence.

flow.do: 1. Label the chairs: 'Yes, plants feel', 'These are responses, and feeling needs a brain', and 'Nobody can test this yet'. 2. Your child writes five facts from this unit on five slips, one fact on each. 3. Read the slips aloud.
flow.say: A debate needs evidence. Write five things that plants have been shown to do. We will use the same facts in every chair.
flow.kid: Label three chairs. Write five facts about what plants do, one on each slip.
flow.parent: Useful facts: a plant sends electrical signals. A plant tells a bite from a cut. A touch-me-not stops folding for harmless drops. Sleeping gases stop a touch-me-not from folding. A plant has no brain or nerve cells.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Chairs. Here you label the chairs and write down five facts.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits in the first chair for two minutes and argues for that view, using the slips. 2. You sit in another chair and answer back. 3. Your child moves to the second chair, and then the third, and does the same.
flow.say: In each chair, argue as if you held that view. Use the facts. I will argue against you from another chair.
flow.kid: Sit in each chair for two minutes. Argue for that chair's view. Use your five facts.
flow.parent: The same fact can serve two chairs. 'Sleeping gases work on plants' can mean that plants feel, or that these gases simply stop ions moving in any cell. Point this out if your child does not. A child working alone can write three short speeches.
flow.context: This is the main part of Three Chairs. Here you argue for each of the three views in turn.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to sit in the chair they agree with most today. 2. Ask which fact mattered most. 3. Ask what new evidence would make them move.
flow.say: Which chair is yours today? Which fact put you there? What would someone have to show you to move you?
flow.kid: Sit in the chair you agree with most. Which fact put you there? What could move you?

check.q: Which of these is evidence that can be used in a debate about what plants feel?
options: A touch-me-not in ether fumes stops folding
Plants are obviously just green machines
Everybody knows flowers are happy in the sun
check.why: The first is something that was measured, and anyone can repeat it. The other two are opinions, said as if they were facts. Both sides of a debate may use the same evidence and still read it differently.

flow.context: This is the last step of Three Chairs. Here you choose the view you agree with most and say what could change your mind.

projects.title: The Music Claim: test a popular belief fairly
projects.context: Many people say that plants grow better with music. In this ten-day project you test that claim on moong seedlings, with a control cup. Then you decide what your result shows and what it does not show.

materials.item: whole green moong seeds
paper cups of the same size, filled with soil
cardboard boxes or buckets of the same size, big enough to cover a cup
a phone or a radio that can play music
a ruler, a marker pen and a notebook

schedule.what: Soak 30 moong seeds overnight. Decide what difference would count as 'music helps'.
Plant 12 seeds in each cup. Mark the cups M and Q. Stand both at a bright window.
Half an hour under the boxes: cup M with music, cup Q in quiet. Then back to the window.
Half an hour under the boxes: cup M with music, cup Q in quiet. Then back to the window.
Half an hour under the boxes: cup M with music, cup Q in quiet. Then back to the window.
Half an hour under the boxes: cup M with music, cup Q in quiet. Then back to the window.
Half an hour under the boxes: cup M with music, cup Q in quiet. Then back to the window.
Half an hour under the boxes: cup M with music, cup Q in quiet. Then back to the window.
Measure every shoot with the letters covered. Find the means and write what the test shows.

projects.record: Write down on day 1 what difference would count. On day 10, write the ten heights for each cup, the two means, the tallest and the shortest shoot in each cup, and one sentence on what the test shows.

setup.art: Two paper cups of young moong seedlings at a window, one marked M and one marked Q.
setup.caption: 1. Grow two cups of moong that are the same in every way. Mark them M and Q.

setup.art: A cardboard box turned upside down over a cup of seedlings and a phone playing music, with the phone a little way from the cup.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, cover cup M with a box for half an hour, with a phone playing music inside.

setup.art: In another room, the same kind of box turned upside down over the second cup, with no phone.
setup.caption: 3. Cover cup Q with the same kind of box in a quiet room for the same half hour.

setup.art: A child measuring seedlings in two cups whose letters are covered with paper strips.
setup.caption: 4. On day 10, measure every shoot without knowing which cup is which.

flow.do: 1. Soak 30 moong seeds in water overnight. 2. Ask your child whether they think music helps plants grow, and why. 3. Agree how big a difference in mean height would count, and write it down.
flow.say: Many people say music helps plants grow. Do you think so? Why? Before we test it, how big a difference would convince you?
flow.kid: Soak 30 moong seeds. Do you think music helps plants? Say why. Write what difference would convince you.
flow.parent: Deciding in advance what counts is what careful scientists do. It stops us from calling any small difference a success afterwards. One centimetre in the means is a sensible bar.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Music Claim. Here you soak the seeds and decide what result would count.

flow.do: 1. Poke three holes in the bottom of each cup and fill both with damp soil. 2. Plant 12 seeds in each cup, one finger-joint deep. 3. Mark one cup M for music and one Q for quiet. 4. Stand both at a bright window and give each two tablespoons of water a day.
flow.say: The cups must be the same in every way except the music. What things do we need to keep the same?
flow.kid: Fill two cups with damp soil. Plant 12 seeds in each. Mark them M and Q. Water both each day.

ask.q: What must be the same for both cups?
good: The seeds, the soil, the water and the light.
The time they spend under a box.

flow.context: This is day 2 of the Music Claim. Here you plant two cups of moong that are the same.

flow.do: 1. Once a day, cover cup M with a box, with the phone playing music 20 centimetres from the cup. 2. Cover cup Q with the other box in another room, with no phone. 3. After 30 minutes, put both cups back at the window. 4. Swap their places at the window each day.
flow.say: Both cups sit in the dark for the same half hour. So what is the only difference between them?
flow.kid: Cover cup M with a box and play music inside. Cover cup Q in a quiet room. After 30 minutes, put both back.
flow.parent: A phone gets warm, so keep it from touching the cup. Use the same music at the same loudness each day. On day 4, pull out the smallest shoots until each cup has 10.
flow.context: This step of the Music Claim lasts six days. Here one cup gets half an hour of music a day and the other gets quiet.

flow.do: 1. Cover the letters and ask someone to measure every shoot. 2. Find the mean for each cup. 3. Write the tallest and the shortest shoot in each cup. 4. Compare the difference in the means with the difference you agreed on day 1. 5. Your child writes one sentence on what the test shows.
flow.say: Is the difference between the cups bigger than the difference between shoots inside one cup? Did it reach the bar we set on day 1?
flow.kid: Measure every shoot with the letters covered. Find both means. Is the difference as big as you said on day 1?

ask.q: Suppose the cups come out the same. Does that prove plants sense no sound at all?
good: No. It shows only that this music did not change the height of moong in six days.
Other tests have found that plants respond to the shaking made by a chewing caterpillar.

flow.parent: Most careful tests find no clear effect of music on growth, so expect two similar means. That is a real result, and a good one to write up. Plants do sense vibrations, but that is different from growing better with songs.

check.q: Two cups of seedlings differ by 2 millimetres on average. Inside each cup, shoots differ by 3 centimetres. What can you say?
options: The test shows no clear difference
check.why: Shoots in one cup differ from each other far more than the two means differ. So a gap of 2 millimetres could easily be chance. The honest report is 'no clear difference in this test'. Choosing 'clearly helped' usually means looking only at the means and not at the spread.

flow.context: This is day 10 of the Music Claim. Here you measure both cups and decide what the test shows.

challenges.title: The Growth Magnifier: watch a shoot grow within one hour
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. A young moong shoot grows about half a millimetre in an hour, which is too little to see on a ruler. J.C. Bose built machines that magnified a plant's growth thousands of times. Here you build a simple magnifier from things at home.
challenges.problem: Build something that turns one hour of a moong shoot's growth into a movement of at least 3 millimetres, so that you can see and measure it.
constraints: The shoot must not be hurt or pulled out of the soil.
You must be able to say how many times your magnifier enlarges the growth.
materials: a cup with a young moong shoot 3 to 8 centimetres tall
a phone torch or a small torch
a sheet of white paper and sticky tape
a ruler or a measuring tape
a drinking straw or a thin stick about 30 centimetres long
a pin, some thread and a paper clip
books to make two small piles
general: Stand a ruler beside the shoot and mark the height every hour for a day.
Take a phone photo every ten minutes from exactly the same place, then flick through the photos.
Stick a tiny paper flag on the tip of the shoot, so that the top is easier to see.
creative: A shadow magnifier. In a dim room, put a torch 20 centimetres from the shoot, so that the shoot's shadow falls on paper taped to a wall 2 metres from the torch. The shadow of the tip moves ten times as far as the tip.

A lever. Push a pin through a straw 3 centimetres from one end, and rest the pin across two piles of books. Tie the short end to the shoot tip with thread. The long end moves nine times as far as the short end.
Two levers, one moving the next. J.C. Bose's crescograph worked this way and magnified growth up to 10,000 times.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own growth magnifier. Draw it, build it and test it for one hour. How many times does it magnify? How do you know?

setup.art: A phone torch propped in a tumbler on a table in a dim room, shining past a single moong shoot in a cup so that a large shadow of the shoot falls on white paper taped to the wall.
setup.caption: 1. Shine a torch past the shoot so that the shadow falls on paper on the wall.

setup.art: A child marking the top of the shoot's shadow on the paper with a pencil, with earlier marks below it labelled 0, 20 and 40 minutes.
setup.caption: 2. Mark the top of the shadow every 20 minutes.

setup.art: A drinking straw balanced on a pin across two piles of books, with a thread from its short end tied to the tip of a moong shoot and its long end pointing at a ruler.
setup.caption: 3. Or build a lever: the long end moves nine times as far as the short end.

flow.do: 1. Stand a ruler beside the shoot and read the height. 2. Ask whether your child expects to see any growth in one hour, and why. 3. Read the problem and the three rules together.
flow.say: This shoot is growing right now. Can we see it grow? How could we make a tiny movement look bigger?
flow.kid: Measure the shoot. Will you see any growth in one hour? Say why. Read the problem.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Growth Magnifier. Here you measure the shoot and read the problem.

flow.do: 1. Tape white paper to a wall. 2. Stand the cup 180 centimetres from the wall. 3. Prop the torch 20 centimetres behind the shoot, so that it is 2 metres from the wall. 4. Darken the room and mark the top of the shadow.
flow.say: The wall is ten times as far from the torch as the shoot is. So how many times bigger is the shadow's movement than the shoot's?
flow.kid: Tape paper to the wall. Put the torch 20 cm behind the shoot. Darken the room. Mark the top of the shadow.

ask.q: The torch is 20 centimetres from the shoot and 200 centimetres from the wall. How many times does the shadow magnify?
good: Ten times, because 200 divided by 20 is 10.

flow.parent: Prop the torch in a tumbler of rice so that it cannot move. Switch it on only to make each mark. A shoot left in torchlight for an hour starts to lean towards the light.
flow.context: This step of the Growth Magnifier builds a shadow magnifier with a torch and a wall.

flow.do: 1. Come back after 20, 40 and 60 minutes. 2. Each time, switch on the torch and mark the top of the shadow. 3. Measure how far the mark has moved in the hour. 4. Divide by 10 to find the real growth.
flow.say: How far did the shadow move? Divide by ten. That is how much the shoot grew while we were away.
flow.kid: Mark the shadow after 20, 40 and 60 minutes. Measure how far it moved. Divide by 10.
flow.wait: Mark the shadow after 20, 40 and 60 minutes
flow.parent: Expect the shadow to move 3 to 10 millimetres in an hour on a warm day. Shoots grow more slowly in cold weather and when the soil is dry.
flow.context: This step of the Growth Magnifier takes an hour. Here you mark the shadow three times.

flow.do: 1. Your child designs a magnifier of their own and draws it. 2. They build it, or the lever, and test it. 3. They work out how many times it magnifies.
flow.say: Now design your own. What will you change? How will you find out how many times it magnifies?
flow.kid: Design your own magnifier. Draw it and build it. Work out how many times it magnifies.
flow.parent: For the lever, hang a paper clip on the short end until the straw almost balances. Then the thread only just tugs the shoot.

check.q: A torch is 10 centimetres from a shoot and 100 centimetres from a wall. The shadow tip moves 5 millimetres. How much did the shoot grow?
check.why: The wall is 10 times as far from the torch as the shoot is, so the shadow moves 10 times as far as the tip. 5 millimetres divided by 10 is half a millimetre. Choosing 5 millimetres forgets that the shadow is magnified.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Growth Magnifier. Here you design and test your own magnifier.

challenges.title: Which Path? Design the test that tells air, soil and fungus apart
challenges.context: This is a design challenge on paper. Two bean plants grow in one pot. When aphids attack one plant, the other gets ready for aphids as well. The warning could have travelled through the air, through the soil water, or along fungal threads. You design the experiment that finds out which.
challenges.problem: Design an experiment that shows which path the warning took between two bean plants in one pot: the air, the soil water or the fungal threads.
constraints: Each test must block one path and leave the other two open.
There must be a control pot in which nothing is blocked.
Each kind of pot must be repeated at least five times.
materials: to build a model: two paper cups, a clear plastic bag, a piece of thin cloth and a piece of card
general: Tie a clear plastic bag over the attacked plant, to block the air path.
Grow the two plants in separate pots, to block every underground path at once.
Push a solid plastic sheet down the middle of the pot.
creative: Use two kinds of mesh. One has holes about half as wide as a hair, which lets fungal threads through and stops roots. The other is far finer, and stops the threads but lets water through.
Grow each plant inside a mesh tube, and give some tubes a small turn every day. The turn snaps the fungal threads and leaves the soil water as it was.
Fill some pots with soil that was heated first, so that the soil holds no living fungus.
challenges.your_turn: Now draw your own experiment. Show every kind of pot, say which path each one blocks, and say what result would point to the air, the soil water or the fungus.

setup.art: A pot with two bean plants, one covered in small green aphids, with three arrows between the plants labelled 'air', 'soil water' and 'fungal threads', each with a question mark.
setup.caption: 1. One plant is attacked and the other gets ready. Three paths are possible.

setup.art: Four pots in a row: one plain, one with a plastic bag over one plant, one with a mesh wall in the soil, and one with a solid wall in the soil.
setup.caption: 2. Design pots that each block one path, and a control pot that blocks none.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem aloud. 2. Your child draws the pot with two plants and three arrows for the three paths. 3. For each path, ask what could block that path alone.
flow.say: The news got across somehow. There are three possible paths. For each one, what could we put in the way?
flow.kid: Draw two plants in one pot. Draw three arrows: air, soil water and fungus. What could block each?
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Path? Here you draw the three paths a warning could take.

flow.do: 1. Look at the three usual ideas together. 2. For each idea, ask which paths it blocks and which it leaves open. 3. Ask which idea cannot tell the soil water from the fungal threads.
flow.say: A solid wall in the soil stops the warning. Does that tell us whether the news went by water or by threads? Why not?
flow.kid: Read the three usual ideas. Which paths does each one block? Which idea blocks two paths at once?

ask.q: Why can a solid wall in the soil not tell the soil water from the fungal threads?
good: It blocks both at the same time.
If the warning stops, we do not know which of the two carried it.

flow.parent: The key idea is to block one path at a time. A bag blocks only the air. A wall or separate pots block both underground paths together, so they cannot separate them.
flow.context: This step of Which Path? looks at the usual ideas and what each one can and cannot show.

flow.do: 1. Read the creative ideas together. 2. Your child draws a full design, with a control pot and five of each kind. 3. Your child writes what each possible result would mean.
flow.say: Now make your own design. Which pot is the control? What result would tell you the fungus carried the news?
flow.kid: Draw your own design. Include a control pot. Write what each result would mean.
flow.parent: In 2013 Zdenka Babikova and her team did this with bean plants and aphids. The warning passed through a mesh that let fungal threads through. It did not pass through a finer mesh that stopped the threads but let water through.

check.q: A warning passes through a mesh that lets fungal threads through. A finer mesh that lets only water through stops it. Which path carried the warning?
check.why: Water could cross both meshes, but the warning crossed only the one that let threads through. So the threads were needed. The air path was the same in both pots, so the air cannot explain the difference.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Path? Here you draw your own design and say what each result would mean.

worksheets.title: Plant signals: paths, partners and the Touch Test (core)

items.p: What must a smell do before we call it a signal?
opts: Be strong enough for people to smell
items.why: A signal carries news that changes what a receiver does. Many signals are far too faint for a person's nose. Choosing 'strong enough for people' puts people at the centre, but most plant signals are not received by us.

items.p: Draw a chewed maize plant, a smell trail and a wasp. Label the sender, the carrier and the receiver.
a: Sender: the chewed maize plant
Carrier: the air, which carries the smell
Receiver: the wasp
items.why: The plant gives off the smell, the air carries it and the wasp responds to it. A strong answer may add that the plant's own far leaves and neighbouring plants are receivers too.
items.art: A blank space for a drawing, with three empty label lines.

items.p: Match each path to an example of news that travels that way.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each path has a different carrier: the plant's own veins, the air, the soil water or a fungus.
pairs: a bitten leaf warns a far leaf of the same plant
a ripe banana makes a raw mango ripen
a witchweed seed senses a jowar root
a ghost plant gets sugar that a tree made

items.p: True or false: a plant needs nerves to send news from one leaf to another.
items.why: False. Plants have no nerves. News travels as waves of electric charge from cell to cell, and as hormones in the sap.

items.p: A partnership between a plant's roots and a fungus is called a ____.
a: mycorrhiza
items.why: Mycorrhiza means 'fungus-root'. More than eight of every ten kinds of land plant have one.

items.p: In a mycorrhiza, sort these by who gives them.
items.a: see items
items.why: The plant makes food from light, so the plant gives sugars and fats. The fungus's fine threads reach far into the soil, so the fungus brings water and minerals.
items: sugars
The plant gives
water
The fungus gives
phosphorus
The fungus gives
fats
The plant gives
other minerals
The fungus gives

items.p: Why can fungal threads collect minerals that roots miss?
opts: They are thin enough for tiny soil gaps
items.why: A fungal thread is many times thinner than a hair, so it enters gaps that no root can. The threads also spread far beyond the roots. No living thing makes minerals from light.

items.p: In the Touch Test, both cups stood at one window and swapped places daily. Why?
items.a: So that both cups got the same light. Then the strokes were the only difference between them.
items.why: A strong answer names light as the thing kept the same, and says that only one thing may differ in a fair test.

items.p: Put the steps of the Touch Test in order.
a: Plant the same number of seeds in two cups
Guess, and measure every shoot
Stroke one cup twice a day for six days
Measure again and compare the means
items.why: Set up two equal cups, record the start, make one change, then measure the result.
items: Stroke one cup twice a day for six days
Measure again and compare the means
Plant the same number of seeds in two cups
Guess, and measure every shoot

items.p: A tree on a windy hilltop is shorter and thicker than the same kind in a valley. Why?
opts: The wind blew the top off
Being bent often changed how the tree grew
items.why: A plant that is bent again and again makes less of the hormone that lengthens stems, and builds thicker walls. Choosing 'blew the top off' treats the shape as damage, but the tree grew that way.

items.p: A touched plant makes less of the ____ that makes stems grow long.
a: hormone
gibberellin
items.why: The hormone is called gibberellin. With less of it, the stem stays shorter.

items.p: True or false: a Venus flytrap closes at the first touch on a trap hair.
items.why: False. The trap closes only when a second touch comes within about 30 seconds. So the trap holds on to the first touch for a short time.

items.p: Draw a fungus living in soil. Show the mushroom and the main body, and label both.
items.a: A mushroom above the ground, and a wide web of fine threads below it, labelled 'mycelium' or 'hyphae'.
items.why: A strong drawing makes the web of threads much bigger than the mushroom. A drawing with only a mushroom shows the common idea that the mushroom is the whole fungus.
items.art: A cross-section of soil with a line for the ground and blank space above and below it.

items.p: Cabbage plants flower only after weeks of cold. What does that tell you about plants and the past?
items.a: The plant's body keeps a record of the cold. Something changed during the winter and stayed changed, so the plant flowers months later.
items.why: A strong answer says that the response today depends on something that happened long before.

items.p: Three of these are real paths for plant signals. Which one is not?
items.why: Plants have no nerves. They send news through the air, inside their bodies as electrical and chemical signals, and from their roots into the soil.
opts: Through the air as a smell
Inside the plant as an electrical signal
Through the soil from the roots

worksheets.title: Evidence and controls in plant experiments (stretch)

items.p: Wasps come to maize chewed by caterpillars, but not to maize torn by hand. What does that show?
opts: Wasps look for holes in leaves
The plant tells a bite from a tear
items.why: Both plants are damaged, but only the chewed one brings wasps. So the plant's response differs. Caterpillar spit in the wound makes the plant give off a different smell. If wasps looked for holes, torn leaves would bring them too.

items.p: A witchweed seed sprouts only when a jowar root is near. How does the seed know?
items.a: The root lets out a chemical into the soil. The seed has receptors for that chemical, and sprouts only when it arrives.
items.why: A strong answer names a chemical from the root as the carrier. It may add that the root makes this chemical to call helpful fungi.

items.p: The heights of ten stroked seedlings add up to 110 centimetres. What is their mean height, in centimetres?
items.why: The mean is the total divided by the number of seedlings. 110 ÷ 10 = 11 centimetres.

items.p: Why should the person measuring the seedlings not know which cup was stroked?
opts: They might stroke the wrong cup
Hopes can shift a measurement without anyone meaning to
items.why: A person who expects the stroked cup to be shorter may read the ruler a little low for that cup. Measuring without knowing removes that risk.

items.p: True or false: when one scientist reports a result, the question is settled.
items.why: False. Other scientists must replicate the test. A result that comes out again in other laboratories can be trusted more.

items.p: Sort these claims: agreed by most scientists, or still debated.
items.a: see items
items.why: The first three have been measured many times. The other three rest on a few studies, or on a question that nobody can yet test.
items: Plants send electrical signals
Agreed
Most plants live joined to fungi
Agreed
Touch makes plants grow shorter and thicker
Agreed
Old trees feed seedlings through fungi in forests
Still debated
Pea seedlings can link a breeze with light
Still debated
Feeling needs a brain
Still debated

items.p: A trained touch-me-not folds for a shake but not for a drop. Why does this rule out tiredness?
items.a: A tired plant could not fold at all. This plant folded for the shake, so the plant had the energy to fold and had stopped only for the drop.
items.why: A strong answer says what tiredness would predict, and that the opposite happened.

items.p: Two forest scientists disagree about big trees and fungal threads.
items.a: A strong answer picks one view and gives its evidence: marked carbon did move between trees, or very few forest studies found a gain for seedlings. It then says what the other side has right, and names a measurement that would help, such as comparing seedlings with and without a link to the network.
items.why: This is a real and current disagreement. Both scientists accept that the networks exist. They differ on how much they matter.

views.says: Marked carbon moved from big trees to shaded seedlings through fungi. Foresters should keep the old trees, because they feed the young ones.
The amounts of carbon were small, and in many tests the seedlings grew no better. We should not tell this story as a fact until it is measured in more forests.

items.ask: Which view do you find stronger, and why? Then say what measurement could change your mind.

items.p: Responding less and less to a harmless thing that keeps happening is called ____.
a: habituation
items.why: Habituation is the simplest kind of learning. It saves the energy of responding to something that does not matter.

items.p: A plant's warning wave moves 1 millimetre a second. How long does it take to reach a leaf 6 centimetres away?
items.why: 6 centimetres is 60 millimetres. At 1 millimetre a second, that takes 60 seconds. Choosing 6 seconds forgets to change centimetres into millimetres.

items.p: Draw two plants in one pot, joined by fungal threads. Mark where a mesh would block the threads.
items.a: Two plants with roots, fine threads running between the roots, and a mesh drawn as a wall in the soil between the two plants.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the mesh right across the soil between the plants. The mesh reaches from the top of the soil to the bottom of the pot, so no thread can go round.
items.art: An empty pot drawn in cross-section, with soil and space for two plants.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are the words scientists use when they test whether plants learn and signal.
pairs: responding faster after meeting a danger once
the part of a test where the change is not made
to do an experiment again to check the result
a chemical that drifts through the air as a smell
a part of a cell that fits one kind of stimulus

items.p: Put these in order, from the fastest to the slowest.
a: A nerve signal in a person
The signal that folds a touch-me-not leaf
The warning wave in a small plant
A stem growing thicker after touch
items.why: A nerve signal travels up to 100 metres a second. The touch-me-not signal travels 2 to 3 centimetres a second. The warning wave travels about 1 millimetre a second. A change in growth takes days.
items: The warning wave in a small plant
A stem growing thicker after touch
A nerve signal in a person
The signal that folds a touch-me-not leaf

items.p: True or false: a ghost plant shows that sugar can pass from a tree to another plant through a fungus.
items.why: True. A ghost plant has no chlorophyll and makes no food. All their sugar was made by trees and arrives through a fungus joined to both.

items.p: A friend says plants do not respond, because they do not move. Give two pieces of evidence against this.
items.a: Any two of these. Stroked seedlings grow shorter and thicker. A bitten leaf warns far leaves within two minutes. A chewed plant gives off a smell that brings wasps. A touch-me-not folds when touched.
items.why: A strong answer gives evidence, and may add that most plant responses are changes in growth or chemistry, which are slow or cannot be seen.

worksheets.title: Reasoning about plant signals, learning and feeling (challenge)

items.p: Plan a fair test of this claim: 'Seedlings grow taller if you talk to them.' Name the control.
items.a: Grow two equal cups of seedlings with the same soil, water and light. Talk to one cup for the same time each day. The other cup is the control: it spends the same time in the same kind of place with no talking. Measure all the seedlings without knowing which cup is which, and compare the means.
items.why: A strong answer keeps everything the same except the talking. It may also notice that a talking person breathes out carbon dioxide and moves the air, so the control needs a person sitting silently nearby.

items.p: Is a damaged plant's smell a warning to neighbouring plants, or do the neighbours overhear it?
items.a: A strong answer picks one view and uses evidence: neighbours do respond and are eaten less, but the sender competes with them for light and water. It then says what the other view has right. It may say that the smell is first a signal to the plant's own leaves and to wasps.
items.why: Scientists really do disagree here. Everyone accepts that the smell is given off and that neighbours respond. The argument is about whom the smell is for.

views.says: It is a warning. The neighbours get ready, and they are eaten less. Plants growing side by side are often close relatives, so warning them helps the family.
It is overheard. A plant gains nothing by helping a rival for light and water. The smell is for the plant's own far leaves and for wasps.

items.ask: Which view do you find stronger, and why? Then say what the other scientist has right.

items.p: In a pot, a warning passes between plants. A mesh that blocks fungal threads but not water stops it. What follows?
opts: The warning went through the air
The warning went through the soil water
The warning needed the fungal threads
items.why: Water still crossed the mesh, and the air was not blocked, yet the warning stopped. The only thing that changed was the threads. So in that pot the threads were needed.

items.p: In the game Under the Forest, sharing saved the shaded seedlings. Why is that not evidence about real forests?
items.a: The game follows rules that we wrote. It shows what would happen if the idea were true. Only measurements in a real forest can show whether enough sugar really moves.
items.why: A strong answer separates a model from a measurement, and says what would need to be measured.

items.p: Untouched seedlings average 15 centimetres and stroked ones 12. The difference is what fraction of the untouched height?
items.why: The difference is 15 − 12 = 3 centimetres. 3 out of 15 is one fifth. So the stroked seedlings are one fifth shorter.

items.p: True or false: a result that fits two explanations equally well helps you choose between them.
items.why: False. To choose, you need a result that one explanation predicts and the other does not. That is why the shake test was needed after the drops.

items.p: Draw a caterpillar's bite and the warning reaching a far leaf. Label glutamate, calcium and hormone.
items.a: A bitten leaf with 'glutamate' at the wound, a wave marked 'calcium' along the veins, and 'hormone' at the far leaf.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the three steps in order: glutamate spills at the wound, a calcium wave travels along the veins, and the far leaf makes a defence hormone.
items.art: An outline of a small plant with one bitten leaf and one far leaf.

items.p: Glutamate carries signals in your brain and in a bitten leaf. What does that suggest about living things?
items.a: Plants and animals probably inherited this way of signalling from a shared ancestor, a single cell that lived more than a billion years ago. So signalling between cells is older than brains.
items.why: A strong answer links the shared chemical to a shared ancestor, and says that this is an idea drawn from comparing living things.

items.p: Touch-me-nots were dropped many times. Sort each result: does it fit 'learned' only, or both 'learned' and 'tired'?
items.a: see items
items.why: A tired plant could not fold for a shake, and would recover with rest. So those two results fit 'learned' only. The other two fit both ideas, so they do not tell us which idea is right.
items: The plants fold for a shake straight after the drops
Fits 'learned' only
The plants stay open for a drop after six days of rest
Fits 'learned' only
The plants stop folding after many drops
Fits both ideas
Plants in dim light stop folding sooner
Fits both ideas

items.p: A fungus sends more minerals to the root that gives more sugar. What does this suggest?
opts: The fungus acts for their own gain
items.why: The fungus rewards the root that pays best, which helps the fungus. So the fungus is a partner with their own needs, not a pipe that the tree controls.

items.p: Two careful scientists test pea seedlings. One finds learning and the other does not. What should happen next?
items.a: More scientists should repeat the test, with many seedlings, and measure without knowing which seedlings were trained. Until then the honest answer is 'not shown yet'.
items.why: A strong answer does not simply pick the scientist it likes. It asks for more tests and accepts 'we do not know yet' for now.

items.p: Put the steps of a maize plant's call for help in order.
a: A caterpillar's spit enters the wound
The plant senses the spit
The plant makes new smell chemicals
Wasps follow the smell to the plant
Wasps lay eggs in the caterpillar
items.why: The plant must sense the spit before making the special smell, and the wasps can come only after the smell is in the air.
items: Wasps follow the smell to the plant
The plant senses the spit
Wasps lay eggs in the caterpillar
A caterpillar's spit enters the wound
The plant makes new smell chemicals

items.p: Draw a jowar root, a chemical in the soil and a witchweed seed. Label sender, carrier and receiver.
a: Sender: the jowar root
Carrier: the chemical in the soil water
Receiver: the witchweed seed
items.why: A strong answer may add a second receiver: the helpful fungus that the root was calling in the first place.
items.art: A blank cross-section of soil with space for a drawing and three label lines.

items.p: A plant that has met a danger once responds faster the next time. This is called ____.
a: priming
items.why: Priming is one way a plant's body keeps information about the past.

items.p: You cannot measure a friend's feelings. Name two clues you use, and say whether a plant gives each.
items.a: Clues include what she says, what she does, and that her body is like mine. A plant does not speak. A plant does respond to harm and to touch. A plant's body is very unlike mine.
items.why: A strong answer sees that we judge feeling from behaviour and from likeness, and that plants give the first kind of clue and not the second. It does not have to reach a verdict.

quiz.p: A ripe banana's gas makes a nearby mango ripen. What is the carrier of this signal?
quiz.why: The banana is the sender and the mango is the receiver. The gas travels through the air, so the air is the carrier.

quiz.p: How does news travel from a bitten leaf to a far leaf of the same plant?
opts: As electrical and chemical signals in the veins
quiz.why: A wave of electric charge and calcium passes from cell to cell along the veins. Plants have no nerves, though the signal is partly electrical, as a nerve signal is.

quiz.p: Wasps arrive at a plant that caterpillars are chewing. What led them there?
opts: A smell the chewed plant gave off
quiz.why: A chewed plant gives off volatiles, and the wasps have receptors for them. The caterpillars are often hidden, so the wasps are not using their eyes.

quiz.p: In a mycorrhiza, what does the plant give the fungus?
quiz.why: A fungus has no chlorophyll and cannot make food from light. The plant gives sugars and fats, and the fungus brings water and minerals such as phosphorus.

quiz.p: True or false: most kinds of land plant live joined to fungi.
quiz.why: True. More than eight of every ten kinds do. Mustard, cabbage and palak are among the few that do not.

quiz.p: In a fair touch test, what is the cup of untouched seedlings for?
opts: It is the control to compare with
It is for next week's test
quiz.why: The control shows how the seedlings grow without the change. Only by comparing with it can you tell what the strokes did.

quiz.p: Seedlings are stroked every day for a week. How do they usually grow?
quiz.why: Repeated touch makes a plant produce less of the hormone that lengthens stems and build thicker walls. 'Taller' is a common guess, from the idea that attention helps plants.

quiz.p: Which of these shows that a plant's body keeps information about the past?
opts: A flytrap closes only on a second touch
quiz.why: To close on the second touch, the trap must hold on to the first touch for some seconds. The other three say nothing about the past.

quiz.p: After many harmless drops, touch-me-nots are shaken sideways and they fold. Which idea does the shake test?
opts: Whether the plants were simply tired
quiz.why: If the plants were tired, they could not fold for the shake either. They folded, so tiredness is ruled out.

quiz.p: A surprising result is reported once. What makes scientists trust it more?
opts: Others repeat it and get the same result
quiz.why: A result that other laboratories can replicate is much less likely to be a fluke or a mistake. Fame and excitement are not evidence.

quiz.p: What is still debated about fungal networks in forests?
opts: How much food and news they carry between trees
quiz.why: Everyone accepts that the networks exist. Scientists disagree about how much sugar and how many warnings pass through them in real forests, and whether seedlings gain from it.

applications: Push-pull farming. In East Africa, farmers plant desmodium between rows of maize. The smell of desmodium drives stem-borer moths away, and chemicals from desmodium roots stop witchweed. Zeyaur Khan, a scientist born in India, led this work in Kenya.
Farmers and nurseries add mycorrhizal fungi to the soil when they plant seedlings. The fungi help young plants take up phosphorus and water.
Plant nurseries brush trays of tomato and other seedlings with a bar or a sheet each day. The touched seedlings grow shorter and sturdier, and survive planting out better.
Gardeners tie a young tree loosely to a stake, so that the trunk can sway. A trunk that sways grows thicker.
Farmers sow a 'trap crop' such as cotton in a field full of witchweed seeds. The cotton roots make the seeds sprout, and the seedlings die without a host.
Maize roots attacked by beetle grubs give off a smell that calls tiny worms, and the worms kill the grubs. Some modern kinds of maize had lost this smell, and scientists have bred it back in.
Engineers are building electronic 'noses' that sense the damage smells of crops. Such a sensor could warn a farmer of pests before any damage can be seen.

open_questions.q: In a real forest, how much food and how many warnings pass from plant to plant through fungal threads?
open_questions.why_open: Mapping the threads between real trees is very hard. Only a few forests have been studied, and the results do not agree.

open_questions.q: When food moves through a fungal network, who decides where it goes: the tree, the fungus, or nobody?
open_questions.why_open: In laboratory dishes, fungi send more minerals to the roots that pay more sugar. Nobody has been able to follow such choices in a forest.

open_questions.q: Can plants learn to link two things, as a dog links a bell with food?
open_questions.why_open: One study of pea seedlings said yes. A larger repeat of the study did not find it. More tests are needed.

open_questions.q: Where in a plant's body is a habit kept, when a touch-me-not goes on staying open for a month?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody has found what changes inside the plant. It may be calcium, chemical tags on genes, or something not yet thought of.

open_questions.q: What, if anything, is it like to be a plant?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody knows how any body gives rise to feeling, not even a human brain. So there is no test yet that could settle it for a plant.
