maths.problem: In the Touch Test, the ten untouched seedlings measured 14, 15, 13, 16, 14, 12, 15, 14, 13 and 14 centimetres. What is their mean height?
maths.explain: Add the ten heights: 14 + 15 + 13 + 16 + 14 + 12 + 15 + 14 + 13 + 14 = 140. Divide by the number of seedlings: 140 ÷ 10 = 14. So the mean is 14 centimetres.
maths.context: This is about the Touch Test. You grew two cups of moong seedlings, stroked one cup twice a day and measured every seedling.
maths.why_maths: Seedlings in one cup are all a little different. The mean gives one number for the whole cup, so two cups can be compared.

maths.problem: The untouched cup has a mean height of 14 centimetres. The stroked cup has a mean of 10.5 centimetres. What percentage shorter is the stroked cup?
maths.explain: The difference is 14 − 10.5 = 3.5 centimetres. Compare it with the untouched height: 3.5 ÷ 14 = one quarter. One quarter is 25 per cent.
maths.context: This is about the Touch Test, where stroked moong seedlings are compared with untouched ones.
maths.why_maths: A percentage lets you compare your result with someone else's, even if their seedlings were all taller or shorter than yours.

maths.problem: In the Torn Leaf Test there are two katoris. If you only guess, the chance of being right once is one half. What is the chance of guessing right five times in a row?
maths.explain: Each guess halves the chance. One half of one half is one quarter. Go on halving five times: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32. So five lucky guesses in a row would happen about once in 32 tries.
maths.context: This is about the Torn Leaf Test. With your eyes closed, you say which of two katoris holds torn leaves, five times.
maths.why_maths: Working out the chance of a lucky guess tells you how many tries you need before you can trust your nose.

maths.problem: In a Touch Test, the stroked seedlings were between 8 and 13 centimetres tall, with a mean of 11. The untouched ones were between 10 and 16, with a mean of 14. A friend says: 'One stroked seedling is taller than one untouched seedling, so stroking does nothing.' Is she right?
maths.answer: No. The two groups overlap, but the stroked group is 3 centimetres shorter on average.
maths.explain: Seedlings always vary, so the shortest untouched one can be shorter than the tallest stroked one. The question is about the groups, not about single seedlings. The means are 11 and 14, which differ by 3 centimetres. To be surer, she could repeat the test with more seedlings.
maths.context: This is about the Touch Test, in which ten stroked moong seedlings are compared with ten untouched ones.
maths.why_maths: Looking at the spread as well as the mean shows whether a difference between two groups is real or could be chance.

maths.problem: A plant's warning wave travels 1 millimetre each second. A caterpillar bites a leaf, and the farthest leaf is 9 centimetres away. The caterpillar needs 20 minutes to finish the first leaf. How long does the far leaf have to get ready before the caterpillar moves on?
maths.explain: 9 centimetres is 90 millimetres, so the wave takes 90 seconds, which is 1 and a half minutes. 20 minutes take away 1 and a half minutes leaves 18 and a half minutes.
maths.context: This is about How Fast Is the News?, where you moved a finger along a ruler at the speed of a plant's warning wave.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two times shows why a signal that looks slow to us is fast enough for the plant.

maths.problem: In Under the Forest, every move of beans along a thread costs 1 bean for the fungus. A big tree wants a seedling to receive 6 beans. How many beans must leave the big tree if they go in 1 move? In 2 moves? In 6 moves? What is the rule?
maths.answer: 7 beans, 8 beans and 12 beans. The rule is: beans sent = 6 + the number of moves.
maths.explain: Each move loses 1 bean. With 1 move, 7 leave and 6 arrive. With 2 moves, 8 leave and 6 arrive. With 6 moves of 2 beans each, 12 leave and 6 arrive. So fewer, bigger moves waste less.
maths.context: This is about the board game Under the Forest, in which trees pass beans of sugar to shaded seedlings along fungal threads.
maths.why_maths: Finding the rule shows the best way to share in the game. It also shows why any real sharing through a fungus would have a cost.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that plants pass news to each other through the air? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: Until the 1980s, most scientists believed that a plant could respond only to what touched that plant directly. In 1983 two studies challenged this. David Rhoades found that willow trees near caterpillar-eaten willows became worse food for caterpillars. Ian Baldwin and Jack Schultz tore the leaves of young poplars and maples in closed boxes. Undamaged plants that shared only the air made more defence chemicals. Newspapers wrote about 'talking trees', and many scientists laughed. They also pointed out real problems. The tests had few plants, and a disease could have spread between Rhoades's trees. For years the idea was dropped. Then came better tests. In 1990 Ted Turlings showed that wasps follow the smell of chewed maize. In 2000 Richard Karban clipped sagebrush bushes in open country, and the wild tobacco plants beside them were eaten less. In 2007 Martin Heil tied plastic bags round bean leaves. With the bags on, no warning passed. That showed the news was travelling through the air.
how_we_found_out.who: David Rhoades, Ian Baldwin and Jack Schultz, who first reported it. Ted Turlings, Richard Karban, Martin Heil and many others, who tested it properly.
how_we_found_out.when: 1983 (the first reports), 1990 (wasps and maize), 2000 (sagebrush and wild tobacco) and 2007 (the plastic bag test)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a plant can respond only to what touches that plant directly, so nothing can pass from one plant to another through the air. Tests with marked plants in open country, and with plastic bags round leaves, showed that damage smells do pass and that neighbours respond.
how_we_found_out.art: A row of grey sagebrush bushes in dry open country, one with clipped branches, and small tobacco plants beside it with whole leaves, while tobacco plants farther away have holes in their leaves.

roots.context: We have learned that plants send signals through their bodies, through the air and through the soil, and that many other beings receive them. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Torn Leaf Test, torn leaves gave off a smell into the open air, and your nose found them. A nearby plant treats that smell as a warning, a hunting wasp as a guide, and you as a sign of dinner. The leaves sent one smell, and each receiver made a different use of it. So what a signal means depends on who receives it.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a message as having one meaning, fixed by the sender, like a letter in an envelope. A plant's smell goes to everyone downwind. Whether it is a warning, a guide or nothing at all depends on the receptors of whoever meets it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Torn Leaf Test you picked out the torn leaves by smell alone. Wasps follow the smell of caterpillar-chewed maize, and neighbouring plants prime their defences when they receive damage smells. Underground, the root chemical that calls a helpful fungus also wakes the seeds of witchweed.

three.who_am_i: You are a receiver too. Your nose and tongue use receptors, as a plant's cells do. You notice only the news you have receptors for.
three.what_is_life: Every living cell senses and responds. No living being has been found who does not. Brains and nerves are one way of doing it, and a fast one.
three.what_is_this_world: The air and the soil are full of chemical news. Most of it passes you by, because other beings have the receptors for it and you do not.

roots.thread: One smell leaves a torn leaf. In a neighbouring plant it becomes a warning, in a wasp a direction to fly, and in you the thought of sambar. The same happens underground, where one root chemical feeds a partnership with a fungus and wakes a witchweed seed. Plants, fungi, insects and people can all read parts of the same chemical world. All of us come down from the same early cells, who already sensed chemicals with receptors. So the many meanings come from one smell, and the many readers come from one family.

teachings.source: Jakob von Uexküll, A Foray into the Worlds of Animals and Humans (1934)
teachings.teaching: Every creature lives in a world made of the few things their body can sense. He called this the creature's 'Umwelt', the world around them. A tick's world holds only a smell, a warmth and a touch.
teachings.link: A wasp's world holds the smell of chewed maize, and yours does not. The same field is a different world to each of you.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, the Buddhist story of the blind men and the elephant, which Jain teachers also tell to explain anekantavada, many-sidedness
teachings.teaching: Several blind men each touch one part of an elephant. One says the elephant is like a pillar and another says like a fan. Each is right about his part and wrong to think it is the whole.
teachings.link: A plant, a wasp and a person each receive one smell and take a different thing from it. No one of them holds the whole of what that smell is.

teachings.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, section 184 (the sage Bhrigu answers Bharadvaja)
teachings.teaching: Bharadvaja asks whether trees are alive and aware. Bhrigu answers that trees feel heat and touch, drink through their roots, and know pleasure and pain. He gives what he has seen as his reasons: leaves wither in heat, and a creeper finds a way round a tree.
teachings.link: Bhrigu argued from what he could see, and had no instruments. The experiments in this unit test the same question with rulers, controls and repeats.

science.text: Insects and neighbouring plants respond to the smells of damaged plants. This has been shown in fields and laboratories since 1990.
Biologists separate a 'signal', which the sender is built to send, from a 'cue', which a receiver simply picks up. Which of these a plant's damage smell is, for neighbouring plants, is not agreed.
Whether there is something it is like to be a plant, and how any body gives rise to feeling, is not known.

other_view.view: A signal does have one true meaning: the job it was shaped for over many generations. Maize plants whose smell brought wasps left more seeds, so the smell is 'for' the wasps and for the plant's own leaves. Other receivers are only eavesdroppers. What they make of the smell is their business, and is not part of what the smell means.

practice.title: One smell, many receivers
practice.say: Take one fresh leaf and tear it under your nose. Close your eyes and breathe in slowly, three times. Notice what the smell makes you think of. Now open your eyes and look around the room. That smell is spreading to every corner. Who else here could receive it? Think of an ant on the floor, a plant on the windowsill and a person in the next room. What might it be to each of them?
practice.kid: Tear one fresh leaf under your nose. Close your eyes. Breathe in three times. What does the smell make you think of? Now look around. Who else could receive this smell? What is it to them?

ask: A torn leaf's smell reached a wasp, a neighbouring plant and you. Was it a message to all three, to one of you, or to nobody?
A seedling grows differently for a week after a one-second touch. Is that remembering? What would you need to see to decide?
You judge what a friend feels from what she does. Should the same rule be used for a plant? Why, or why not?
What news might be passing through this room right now that you have no receptors for?

playtest: The experiments and activities in this unit were reasoned through step by step. They have not yet been tried at home, so please treat amounts and times as a starting point. The Torn Leaf Test (core) works best with curry leaves, tulsi, mint or coriander. Palak and grass smell fainter, so hold the katori close. The Touch Test (core) takes 11 days and needs soil, because seedlings on cotton fall over when they are stroked. Shoots must be 3 to 4 centimetres tall before the first stroke, which can take longer than three days in cold weather. Stroked seedlings usually end 1 to 3 centimetres shorter on average, and single seedlings overlap. If the two means differ by less than half a centimetre, the step says to report that and run four more days. The Drop Test needs a touch-me-not, so it is outside the core path. Tie the marking threads an hour ahead, and expect results to vary from plant to plant. See the Threads grows mould, so the bag stays sealed and goes in the dustbin. Packaged bread can take ten days, and a chapati or an idli is faster. Stroke a Tendril needs a climber and is outside the core path. Old tendrils do not respond. In the Growth Magnifier the torch must not move, and it is switched on only to make each mark, because a shoot leans towards a steady light. The Music Claim will most likely show no clear difference, and the step says that this is a real result. Under the Forest was played through on paper. Without sharing, both seedlings die in round 4. With sharing in moves of three or four beans, all six trees can last eight rounds. A big tree stripped twice in the first two rounds can die, and then the game is played again. The game shows a debated idea, and its last step says so. Which Path? needs 20 cards and four tokens for each player. No part of the core path needs a garden. The dates, names and numbers come from published papers. They were written from memory of those papers and have not yet been checked against them by a person. The three videos were confirmed by title and channel but not watched.
